The Luanda–Dakar–Praia route takes shape

TAAG Angola Airlines, the state-owned carrier with IATA code DT, will begin flying from Luanda to Dakar and onward to Praia on 31 October 2026. The launch comes days after the IATA winter 2026/27 season opens on 25 October 2026, a scheduling window that runs through late March 2027.

The triangular routing adds both Senegal and Cape Verde to TAAG’s international map. Before this expansion, the airline served 12 international destinations from its hub at Luanda Dr António Agostinho Neto International Airport.

TAAG frames the new corridor as a bridge between Angola and the Economic Community of West African States, or ECOWAS, region. The airline says the route contributes to continental integration and connectivity, language that echoes the African Union’s long-standing push for freer skies.

A commercially cautious comeback after a 2016 exit

TAAG is returning to a market it abandoned at the end of 2016, when it suspended Luanda–Praia flights that operated with a stop in São Tomé and Príncipe. The airline declared that earlier service unprofitable, a reminder that political enthusiasm alone does not fill seats.

Cape Verde’s ambassador to Angola, Júlio Morais, has been blunt about the commercial test. He has said trade between the two countries is practically zero because of missing direct air and sea links, and that new flights must be profitable rather than politically driven.

Morais has pointed to feasibility studies focused on the ECOWAS market as the foundation for the resumption. That grounding in demand analysis marks a shift from earlier connectivity efforts that leaned on diplomatic goodwill.

Lusophone hub strategy links Sal and Luanda

Angola and Cape Verde are both members of the Community of Portuguese-Language Countries, known as CPLP, and officials in both capitals see aviation as a tool for deeper Lusophone integration. Cape Verde’s Minister of Tourism and Transport, José Luís Sá Nogueira, has described the archipelago as a strategic hub for distributing passengers and cargo to Europe and the Americas.

The partnership process between TAAG and TACV, Cape Verde’s national carrier, is central to this vision. Officials have discussed using Sal and Luanda as complementary hubs, allowing the two airlines to share traffic across Southern Africa, West Africa, Europe and the Americas.

For Angola, the route supports a broader ambition to diversify an economy still heavily dependent on crude oil. Better air links into West African markets and trans-Atlantic hubs can help Luanda position itself as a logistics and cargo gateway, not just an oil capital.

African air liberalisation in practice

TAAG explicitly places the Luanda–Dakar–Praia route within the framework of the Yamoussoukro Decision and the Single African Air Transport Market, or SAATM. SAATM is a flagship project of the African Union’s Agenda 2063, designed to remove restrictive bilateral air service agreements and let African carriers launch intra-African routes more freely.

The route is a concrete test of whether liberalised markets can support pan-African connections without relying on European or Gulf hubs. By inserting Dakar between Luanda and Praia, TAAG taps into Senegal’s role as a major West African aviation node while opening access to wider ECOWAS passenger flows.

TAAG already serves Abidjan in Côte d’Ivoire and has historically operated Lagos and São Tomé routes. The new corridor deepens that West African footprint and positions the airline as a continental connector rather than a niche carrier tied mainly to Lisbon.

Great-power and regional competition overlay

TAAG’s expansion is not happening in isolation. The airline is in the middle of a two-year transformation programme that has already added Nairobi on 1 September 2025, with Abidjan and Accra targeted for the first quarter of 2026 and Guangzhou planned before summer 2026.

The Guangzhou route highlights China’s deep economic role in Angola, while Lisbon remains TAAG’s top European destination and Porto is being evaluated for year-round service. Once Luanda is better connected to West Africa, Lusophone Atlantic hubs, Europe and China, Angola’s capital becomes a node in a China–Africa–Atlantic trade corridor.

Cape Verde’s mid-Atlantic location also carries strategic weight, with European Union and NATO partners interested in migration routes, maritime security and Atlantic trade. Strengthening civil aviation links through TAAG and TACV reinforces the archipelago’s role as a logistics and monitoring point in a contested ocean space, a theme explored in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The first flight on 31 October 2026 will be an early indicator of demand, but the real test is whether TAAG can sustain the route through the winter season and beyond. Load factors on the Dakar–Praia leg will matter as much as those on the Luanda–Dakar segment.

Investors and travel industry players should watch for any formal announcement on TACV–TAAG joint operations, including shared scheduling or codeshare arrangements. A deeper partnership would signal that the Lusophone hub strategy is moving from rhetoric to commercial reality.

The route also sets up a competitive dynamic with Air Senegal, ASKY Airlines and Royal Air Maroc in West Africa. Whether TAAG can win connecting traffic between Southern Africa and West Africa will determine if this expansion strengthens Luanda’s hub ambitions or remains a symbolic gesture.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does TAAG start flying the Luanda–Dakar–Praia route? TAAG Angola Airlines launches the Luanda–Dakar–Praia route on 31 October 2026, in the opening week of the IATA winter 2026/27 season, which opens on 25 October. Why did TAAG stop flying to Cape Verde before? TAAG suspended its Luanda–Praia route at the end of 2016, declaring it unprofitable after operating with a stop in São Tomé and Príncipe. What is the strategic purpose of the new route? The route supports Angola’s goal of turning Luanda into a regional aviation hub and aligns with the African Union’s Single African Air Transport Market, or SAATM, liberalisation agenda.

World.title: South Africa’s Democratic Alliance Unveils a Quiet Manifesto Strategy
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

South Africa · POLITICS

Key Facts —Manifesto launch: The Democratic Alliance launched its 2024 election manifesto on 17 February 2024, setting out seven apex priorities. —Seven priorities: The party aims to create two million jobs, end load-shedding and water-shedding, halve violent crime, abolish cadre deployment, lift six million people out of poverty, triple Grade 4 reading literacy, and ensure quality healthcare for all. —Coalition reality: The DA entered South Africa’s Government of National Unity after the African National Congress lost its parliamentary majority in the 2024 national election. —Municipal money: The DA’s local-government platform promises to ring-fence water and electricity revenue, publish every contract price including any premium above the lowest qualifying bid, and bring in private operators where councils fail. —Global standing: South Africa is Africa’s largest economy, one of two African members of the G20, alongside the African Union, and a member of BRICS. It held the G20 presidency from December 2024 through November 2025. —Strategic framing: The manifesto doubles as an election platform and a governing blueprint, signalling seriousness to investors while remaining coalition-compatible.

The Democratic Alliance’s manifesto strategy is a coalition-era reform pitch disguised as an opposition programme, built around administrative competence rather than ideological confrontation.

A two-track DA manifesto strategy for a hung parliament

South Africa’s Democratic Alliance (DA) is running a deliberately quiet, two-track manifesto strategy. Publicly, this DA manifesto strategy promises a hard-edged reform agenda aimed at reversing what it calls “state collapse.”

Politically, however, the party packages that agenda in a coalition-compatible way that can appeal beyond its traditional base. The language is built around deliverables and measurable outcomes rather than culture-war provocations.

This dual character matters because South Africa’s political landscape changed fundamentally in 2024. The African National Congress (ANC) fell below 50 percent of the national vote for the first time, forcing the creation of a Government of National Unity that includes the DA.

Seven apex priorities that sound like a governing blueprint

The DA launched its manifesto on 17 February 2024 with seven apex priorities that read more like a cabinet work plan than a protest document. The party promises to create two million jobs, end load-shedding and water-shedding, and halve violent crime.

It also pledges to abolish cadre deployment in favour of merit-based appointments, lift six million people out of poverty, triple the number of Grade 4 learners who can read for meaning, and ensure quality healthcare for all. Every priority is framed as a measurable rescue target.

The manifesto says the DA will “start fixing what is broken in government” by ending cadre deployment, firing corrupt officials, and appointing competent people. That technocratic tone makes the document saleable to business audiences, middle-class voters, and potential coalition partners alike.

Where the money meets the politics: municipal procurement

The DA’s local-government messaging reveals where its reform agenda bites hardest. In its 2026 municipal campaign, the party declares that “public money is never party money” and promises to ring-fence revenue collected for water and electricity exclusively for those services.

It also says municipal accounting officers may be forced to repay losses caused by their actions or inaction. The party further commits to publishing the price of every contract, including any premium above the lowest qualifying bid, and to bringing in private operators where councils cannot deliver.

These pledges are a direct challenge to patronage networks and procurement opacity. In South Africa’s political economy, control over municipal revenue, tenders, and state jobs is the main channel through which political power converts into financial power.

A governance-by-market model that courts investors

Running through the DA manifesto strategy is a clear governance-by-market thread. The party presents the private sector and civil society as partners in rescuing the state, not as adversaries to be regulated or sidelined.

Its older manifesto language tied job creation to growth, labour reform, and skills development. That suggests a pro-investment, pro-management model of state reform rather than a statist redistribution agenda.

For business audiences, the attraction is straightforward. The DA is essentially arguing that better administration can unlock growth, infrastructure maintenance, and service reliability without requiring a wholesale ideological revolution.

Why the DA manifesto strategy echoes beyond South Africa

South Africa is Africa’s largest economy and one of two African members of the G20, alongside the African Union. It assumed the G20 presidency in December 2024, running through November 2025, and remains a prominent BRICS member.

Pretoria uses BRICS and wider Global South diplomacy to push for a more multipolar world order and greater influence for developing countries. Any party in or near power in South Africa is therefore indirectly implicated in global economic governance.

The DA’s emphasis on competence and clean government is not merely domestic technocracy. It is also a bid to make South Africa look governable to international investors, trading partners, and multilateral forums at a moment when the country’s external credibility depends heavily on performance at home, as explored in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch as the coalition era deepens

The DA manifesto strategy is deliberately less ideological than older party messaging, more managerial, and more compatible with government participation. In a South Africa where the battle is increasingly over state capacity, procurement, and public-service delivery, that approach is politically smarter than maximalist rhetoric.

The real test will be whether the party can deliver measurable improvements in the municipalities it controls while maintaining its reformist edge inside a Government of National Unity that has been repeatedly strained by disputes over VAT, the Expropriation Act, and cabinet dismissals. Investors and diplomats will watch local-government procurement reforms closely for signals about the wider investment climate.

The next municipal elections will show whether voters reward a party that promises to publish contract prices and ring-fence service revenue. If they do, the DA’s quiet, clever manifesto strategy may become the template for opposition politics across the region.

The manifesto uses technocratic, measurable language rather than ideological confrontation, making it saleable to coalition partners and business audiences after the ANC lost its majority in 2024. What does the DA promise on municipal procurement? The party pledges to ring-fence water and electricity revenue, publish every contract price including premiums above the lowest qualifying bid, and bring in private operators where councils fail to deliver services.

World.title: The Panama Canal Opened 112 Years Ago Today
World.content:
Twelve years of digging, an estimated 27,500 deaths and roughly $375 million ended quietly on the morning of August 15, 1914, when a single steamship slipped into a lock chamber on Panama’s Caribbean coast and began climbing a staircase of water.

The SS Ancon, a cargo and passenger vessel of the Panama Railroad Company, left Cristóbal at Colón and reached the Pacific port of Balboa about nine hours later. It was the first official transit of the Panama Canal, and it joined the Atlantic and Pacific for the first time in human history.

The ship covered roughly 80 kilometers (50 miles). Electric towing locomotives, still known as mules, guided it through the three chambers of the Gatún Locks, lifting it about 26 meters (85 feet) above sea level and into Gatún Lake.

From there the Ancon crossed the lake and entered the Culebra Cut, the narrow slot carved through the continental divide and the deadliest, most unstable stretch of the entire project. Landslides had swallowed months of work there. On that morning the ship passed through without incident, dropped down through the Pedro Miguel and Miraflores locks, and reached the Pacific.

Chief engineer George W. Goethals, the U.S. Army officer who had driven the project to completion, watched much of it from a railcar running alongside the ship. Senior canal pilot John A. Constantine had the helm.

What was missing was the celebration. Panama had planned an international fleet review, with warships gathering off Virginia and steaming through the new canal to San Francisco for the Panama-Pacific International Exposition. The First World War had begun in Europe two weeks earlier, and the fleet never sailed. The opening of one of the largest engineering projects ever attempted went almost unnoticed outside the isthmus.

The Ancon was not, strictly speaking, the first vessel through. A French-built crane boat, the Alexandre La Valley, had worked its way across in stages during construction and reached the Pacific on January 7, 1914. The Ancon’s sister ship, the Cristóbal, carried a load of cement through on August 3. But the Ancon’s run was the ceremonial one, the transit that opened the waterway to commercial traffic.

The change it produced was immediate and permanent. Ships moving between the east and west coasts of the Americas had until then rounded Cape Horn or threaded the Strait of Magellan, adding thousands of kilometers and weeks of sailing to every voyage, along with some of the worst weather on the planet. The canal erased that detour overnight and cut freight costs across two oceans.

It also handed the United States a strategic instrument. A navy able to shift between the Atlantic and Pacific in days rather than months was a different navy, and Washington held the Canal Zone until the Torrijos-Carter treaties transferred full control to Panama on the last day of 1999.

The waterway is busier now than its builders imagined. Through the first nine months of the 2026 fiscal year, the canal averaged 35 transits a day and logged 10,726 crossings, a 5.2% increase over the same period a year earlier. Ships far larger than the Ancon pass through the expanded neopanamax locks opened in 2016.

The threat to all of it is not congestion but rainfall. The canal runs on fresh water, and every transit drains tens of millions of liters from the lakes that feed the lock chambers. A severe drought in 2023 and 2024 forced the Panama Canal Authority to cut daily transits and restrict how deeply loaded ships could sit, sending ripples through global supply chains and freight rates.

Two wet years followed and restrictions were lifted. That reprieve now looks temporary. Canal Administrator Ricaurte Vásquez Morales has said the probability of a severe El Niño event climbed from 25% in April to 81% by July, and that limits on draft and on the number of daily booking slots are likely to return.

The long-term answer is a reservoir on the Río Indio, approved by the canal’s board in February 2025 at an estimated cost of $1.6 billion. A dam would create a new lake of about 4,600 hectares (11,370 acres), feeding Gatún Lake by gravity through a tunnel of roughly 8.7 kilometers (5.4 miles) and supplying drinking water to more than half of Panama’s population.

Construction is not scheduled to begin until 2027 and would take about six years, putting the reservoir in service around 2032 at the earliest. The canal authority puts the number of residents who would be displaced at roughly 2,000 across 38 farming communities; opposition groups and some published estimates put the figure higher, and the farmers of the Río Indio basin have organized against the project, arguing for the expansion of an existing reservoir on the Bayano River instead.

An environmental impact assessment at Panama’s most stringent review level, including formal public hearings, is due to be presented in the second half of this year. A hundred and twelve years after the Ancon made its unheralded crossing, the canal’s central problem has inverted.

The men who built it fought rock, mud and disease to force a path between two oceans. The people who run it now are fighting to keep enough water in the mountains above it to float the ships through.

World.title: Costa Rica Estate Becomes Refuge for Rare Agami Heron
World.content:
Around 1,000 agami herons have made a private estate in Guatuso their home, creating an unusual concentration of one of the most elusive heron species found in Costa Rica. Its near the Caño Negro wetlands, the property has become an important refuge and breeding site for the birds, prompting researchers, local residents, and the landowners to work together to study and protect the colony.

Researchers from the National Distance Education University (UNED) are monitoring the site and plan to continue carrying out censuses. Their work will focus not only on determining how many herons are present but also on counting nests and chicks to better understand the colony’s reproductive success.

The agami heron ranges from Mexico to South America but is rarely seen because of its secretive behavior and preference for densely vegetated wetland habitats. In Costa Rica, the species is primarily associated with humid areas in the Caribbean region and the Osa Peninsula.

It is also among the most colorful herons in the Neotropics. While many heron species are dominated by white, gray, brown, or dark tones, the agami heron is known for its distinctive and vibrant plumage.

Efforts to study the Guatuso colony began after the property owner contacted UNED and requested assistance in researching the birds. The owner also expressed an interest in investing resources to maintain the environmental conditions that have allowed the colony to establish itself.

The initiative has since expanded beyond scientific monitoring to include environmental education and community participation. People working on the estate are being trained to recognize threats and understand how their activities can affect the areas used by the birds for feeding, resting, and nesting.

For nearby communities, the colony could also become an opportunity to promote birdwatching and nature-based tourism in Katira, particularly because of its proximity to the Caño Negro wetlands. Community leader Odir Rojas Gómez stressed that the presence of such a large colony brings both opportunities and responsibilities.

“We want the communities to be part of its protection and for people who come to learn about it to understand that they are facing a space we must care for future generations,” he said. Researchers, however, warn that increased attention could pose risks if tourism is not carefully managed.

Herons and other waterbirds can be particularly vulnerable to disturbance during nesting periods. Visitors approaching too closely, excessive noise, or a constant human presence can cause adult birds to temporarily leave their nests, potentially exposing eggs and chicks to predators or falls.

For that reason, researchers are considering measures such as establishing minimum viewing distances, using binoculars and telescopes, and creating camouflaged observation areas. The objective is to avoid mass tourism while allowing people to experience the colony without disturbing it. “We don’t want the interest sparked by this gathering to end up becoming a threat,” said Ever Shion Salas, project designer and manager at UNED.

Continued monitoring of adults, nests, and chicks will help researchers determine how the colony develops over time and what conservation measures are necessary to protect this unusual gathering of agami herons.

World.title: Five Costa Rican Surfers Advance at Playa Hermosa WSL Event
World.content:
Five Costa Rican surfers remain in contention at the Garabito Surf City Pro after advancing to the round of 32 at the World Surf League qualifying event on the country’s Central Pacific coast. Jason Torres, Darshan Antequera, Maykol Torres, Carlos “Cali” Muñoz and Sam Reidy made it through Friday’s competition at Playa Hermosa in Garabito, keeping alive the chance of a Costa Rican victory as the event heads into its decisive weekend rounds.

The QS 2000 competition, which runs through Sunday, marks the return of the World Surf League’s Qualifying Series to Costa Rica. Surfers from 19 countries entered the event, including 23 Costa Ricans, with valuable ranking points at stake for competitors trying to move toward the Challenger Series.

Reidy produced one of the strongest Costa Rican performances yesterday, winning his heat with a score of 13.05. He is scheduled to face Chile’s Manuel Selman, Mexico’s Jhonny Corzo and fellow Costa Rican Maykol Torres in the next round. Maykol Torres also won his previous heat, scoring 10.90 while eliminating fellow Costa Ricans Óscar Urbina and Axel Castro along with American Hayden Rodgers.

Muñoz, one of Costa Rica’s most experienced international surfers, won his heat with 12 points. Antequera advanced after finishing second with 11.05, while Jason Torres also moved forward with a second-place finish. The remaining Costa Rican surfers have strong connections to communities along the Pacific coast. Jason Torres and Antequera are from the Garabito area, Maykol Torres and Muñoz represent Parrita, and Reidy comes from the Dominical area in the canton of Osa.

That local presence has added another dimension to an event designed not only as an international competition but also as a showcase for one of Costa Rica’s best-known surfing destinations. Playa Hermosa, just south of Jacó, has long been known for powerful and consistent waves that draw the attention of experienced surfers. The beach was named a World Surfing Reserve in 2020, the first such designation in Central America.

The Garabito Surf City Pro is part of the WSL Qualifying Series and offers 2,000 ranking points to the winners. The competition carries a total prize purse of $24,000 and includes men’s and women’s open divisions. The event also comes as Garabito works to strengthen its identity as a sports and surf-tourism destination. The tournament coincides with the canton’s inclusion in the Surf City Network and is backed locally by tourism and municipal organizations.

For the five Costa Ricans still alive in the men’s competition, however, the goal is to keep advancing and give the home crowd here a local surfer to support deep into the final rounds. Competition continues today at Playa Hermosa, with the event scheduled to conclude Sunday.

World.title: Mother’s Day Is a Full National Holiday in Costa Rica
World.content:
Today is Día de la Madre, and it is a full national holiday in Costa Rica, not just a greeting-card occasion. Public offices are shut, most bank branches are closed, and if you were planning to sort out any paperwork before Monday, that plan is gone. The date does not move. Costa Rica marks Mother’s Day on August 15 every year, unlike the United States, Canada and Mexico, where it falls in May. Newcomers routinely miss it because they are watching for a date in spring.

It also does not get shifted to the nearest Monday. Costa Rica applies no holiday transfers in 2026, so every holiday this year lands on its actual calendar date. Because August 15 is a Saturday, most people on a Monday-to-Friday schedule get no extra day off at all. That matters more than it sounds. If you work Saturdays, today is a holiday you are entitled to, and the pay rules are specific.

If you do not work, you receive your normal pay. If you do work, you are owed double. Any overtime on top of that carries a further 50 percent surcharge on the double-time hour, which is where the familiar “triple pay” figure comes from. How the base pay lands depends on how you are paid.

If your salary is monthly, fortnightly, or weekly in a commercial activity, the holiday is already built into what you receive. Work it, and your employer adds one more day’s ordinary pay to make up the double. In non-commercial work paid weekly or by the hour, the holiday day is paid on top of the days you actually worked.

There is also a rule most people never hear about. Article 149 of the Labor Code prohibits employers from having staff work on holidays at all. The exceptions in Articles 150 and 151 cover activities that cannot simply stop — the reason your local soda is open and the Registro Nacional is not. If your employer asked you in today and you are not in one of those categories, the law was on your side to decline.

Practically, expect the day to feel like a Sunday with more traffic. Restaurants are booked solid; this is one of the busiest dining days of the year here, and walking in without a reservation at lunchtime is optimistic. Many shops open on reduced hours rather than closing outright, so call ahead rather than driving out.

The roads are the part worth planning around. Holiday traffic is heavy today, and it is landing on the same day Tropical Wave 32 crosses the country. The Caribbean slope and Northern Zone are under yellow alert, with rain from early morning and gusts reaching 85 kilometres per hour (53 miles per hour) in the mountains. If you are driving to see family, leave early, check that your route is open, and build in more time than the distance suggests.

One more thing worth checking before the day gets away from you. If you employ anyone — a domestic worker, a gardener, a caretaker — today is a mandatory-pay holiday for them as well, whether or not they come in.

The fixed date is the giveaway to the holiday’s origins. August 15 is the Feast of the Assumption on the Catholic calendar, and Costa Rica folded the civic celebration onto the religious one rather than inventing a floating spring date. That is why the country marks it in the middle of the rainy season, and why almost every family here has a plan B for lunch under a roof.

World.title: U.S. and Costa Rica Discuss Deeper Security Cooperation
World.content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Costa Rican President Laura Fernández today as the two countries look to deepen security cooperation amid growing concern over drug trafficking and organized crime in the region. Rubio called Fernández to reaffirm what the U.S. State Department described as the strong partnership between the United States and Costa Rica.

The two officials discussed opportunities to expand cooperation on security while maintaining close trade and investment ties. The brief U.S. readout did not announce a new security agreement, funding package or specific joint operation, leaving the details of any expanded cooperation unclear. Still, the conversation comes as security has become one of the defining issues of Fernández’s first months in office.

Fernández, who took office on May 8, has pushed a series of proposals intended to give police and prosecutors additional tools against organized crime and repeat offenders. Her administration presented an initial package of six security bills in June and followed it with another group of proposals in late July.

The measures include proposed changes to criminal procedures, police protections, electronic monitoring, criminal records and penalties for certain offenses. Many of the proposals still require approval in the Legislative Assembly. Closer cooperation with Washington would build on an already extensive relationship between the two countries in the fight against drug trafficking.

Costa Rica has long worked with U.S. agencies on maritime drug interdiction, port and border security, police training and investigations targeting international criminal organizations. U.S. officials have identified Costa Rica as an important transit point for cocaine moving north from South America. The Rubio-Fernández conversation also comes during a period of increased U.S. attention to organized crime across Latin America.

Costa Rica participated earlier this year in the U.S.-backed Escudo de las Américas initiative, which brought regional governments together to discuss narcotrafficking, criminal organizations, migration and security cooperation. Former President Rodrigo Chaves attended the initiative’s March summit in Miami shortly before Fernández took office.

For Costa Rica, cooperation with the United States is particularly important at sea since Costa Rica has no standing army, and its security forces include the Coast Guard, Drug Control Police, Public Force and Air Surveillance Service. International trafficking organizations have increasingly used Costa Rica both as a transit route and as a logistics point for cocaine shipments moving through ports and coastal areas.

The issue was highlighted again today when authorities announced the arrest of a Costa Rican police officer and seven other people in connection with an alleged attempt to move 256 packages of cocaine through APM Terminals in Limón. Fernández has made confronting organized crime one of her government’s central priorities, promising a tougher response to narcotrafficking and violent crime while seeking changes to Costa Rica’s policing and justice systems.

Today’s call suggests Washington will remain a major partner in that effort. What remains unanswered is what “deeper” security cooperation will mean in practice. Neither government announced new operations, personnel deployments, equipment transfers or financial commitments following the conversation.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves Immigration Applications Online for Some Foreign Executives
World.content:
Costa Rica has moved several immigration procedures for foreign executives and their families online, allowing eligible applicants to complete and track the process through the Ventanilla Única de Inversión, or One-Stop Investment Window. The new service became available yesterday and is aimed specifically at people connected to companies operating under Costa Rica’s Free Trade Zone Regime.

For now, the online system covers three immigration categories: Free Trade Zone Executives, Dependents of Company Executives and Free Trade Zone Stays. Applicants using the platform can review requirements and applicable regulations, submit their cases, follow the progress of their applications and receive notifications and approvals online.

The system also provides a record of each stage of the process and allows applicants to interact with the government agencies handling their cases. The change is particularly relevant for international companies that regularly bring managers, executives and other specialized personnel into Costa Rica.

The General Directorate of Immigration and Foreigners developed the service with Costa Rica’s foreign trade promotion agency Procomer, with support from the Ministry of Foreign Trade. The immigration procedures have been added to the Ventanilla Única de Inversión, commonly known as VUI, an existing digital platform designed to bring government procedures required by businesses into one system.

The platform already centralizes dozens of processes related to opening, expanding and formally operating companies in Costa Rica. The government has been expanding the platform as part of a broader effort to reduce the amount of paperwork and in-person processing required from companies operating in the country.

For foreign companies, immigration procedures can be an important part of establishing or expanding operations in Costa Rica, particularly when businesses need to relocate executives or specialized employees from other countries. The online system should make it easier for participating companies and their employees to see where an application stands instead of relying entirely on separate communications with government offices.

However, the change does not mean Costa Rica has introduced online processing for all residency applications. The service announced this week applies only to the three designated categories connected to qualifying companies and the Free Trade Zone Regime. Foreign residents applying through other immigration categories should not assume their residency applications can now be submitted through the VUI.

Costa Rica’s Free Trade Zone Regime is a major part of the country’s strategy for attracting foreign investment. Companies operating under the program receive tax and customs incentives in exchange for meeting investment, employment and other requirements. The addition of immigration procedures to the VUI is therefore aimed as much at companies as individual applicants. The government wants businesses bringing foreign talent into Costa Rica to have a more predictable and trackable process.

The three newly available immigration procedures can now be started through the VUI platform.

World.title: International News: Hurricane Lala strengthens to Category 1 as it nears Hawaii’s Big Island
World.content:
International News: Hurricane Lala strengthens to Category 1 as it nears Hawaii’s Big Island

By Zoila Palma: Hurricane Lala strengthened into a Category 1 hurricane on Saturday and began lashing Hawaii’s Big Island with strong winds and heavy rain as it approached what could become a historic landfall.

The storm was packing maximum sustained winds of 75 mph and was located about 120 miles south of Hilo, according to the National Hurricane Center. A 50-mph tropical-storm-force wind gust was also reported near Kealakomo.

A hurricane warning is in effect for the Big Island, with hurricane conditions expected to begin Saturday afternoon. Southern portions of the island are considered most likely to experience hurricane-force winds as Lala’s strongest winds pass near or over land. The storm could also produce dangerous storm surge of up to 1 to 3 feet along parts of the coast, while waves of 8 to 12 feet are expected along some east-facing shores.

The storm’s greatest threat is expected to be torrential rainfall, with more than a foot of rain forecast across much of the Big Island and isolated totals exceeding two feet.

More than 12 inches had already fallen in Keanakolu during the previous 24 hours. The National Hurricane Center warned of life-threatening flash flooding and mudslides, particularly in mountainous areas. Heavy rainfall is expected across Hawaii through Monday, with up to a foot also possible in parts of Maui.

If Lala makes landfall as a hurricane, it would mark the first hurricane to directly strike Hawaii in more than 30 years and the first recorded hurricane landfall on the Big Island.

The last hurricane to make landfall in Hawaii was Category 4 Hurricane Iniki in 1992, which struck Kauai. Tropical Storm Olivia later made landfall on Maui in 2018, marking the island’s first recorded tropical-system landfall.

World.title: International News: Pope Leo XIV urges young people to embrace Christ and call to Holiness
World.content:
International News: Pope Leo XIV urges young people to embrace Christ and call to Holiness

By Zoila Palma: Pope Leo XIV has encouraged young people attending the Third National Youth Day in Monterrey, Mexico, to strengthen their relationship with Christ and embrace their call to holiness.

The gathering is taking place August 15–16, 2026, bringing young Catholics together with their pastors for prayer, reflection and fellowship.

In a message to organizers and participants, Pope Leo described the event as an opportunity for young people to encounter Christ and discover the deeper purpose of their lives. “It is a beautiful opportunity for all of you to meet, together with your pastors, an encounter that springs from communion with Christ,” he said.

The Pope urged participants to live out the words of Jesus, “And you also testify, because you have been with me from the beginning,” from the Gospel of John. He stressed that remaining united with Christ is essential for young people who want to help others find faith, particularly amid challenges such as violence, indifference and a lack of meaning.

Pope Leo also encouraged the young participants to make time for silence and reflection so they can discern what is truly worthwhile in their lives.

World.title: New Mural in Punta Gorda celebrates East Indian heritage and history
World.content:
New Mural in Punta Gorda celebrates East Indian heritage and history

By Zoila Palma: A new mural celebrating the history, heritage and contributions of Belize’s East Indian community was unveiled on August 14 at the Punta Gorda Market and Plaza.

The mural, titled “Remembering Our Past, Reviving Our Roots, and Embracing Our Future as Indians in Belize,” highlights an important chapter of Belize’s multicultural history.

Members of the Institute for Social and Cultural Research (ISCR) joined the unveiling ceremony, which showcased the role of the East Indian community in Belize’s national development.

The mural serves as a public reminder of the country’s diverse cultural heritage and the traditions that continue to shape communities across Belize.

ISCR congratulated artist Jill Burgess for bringing the story to life through her artwork, describing the mural as a meaningful contribution to the cultural and artistic expression of Punta Gorda. The project was made possible through resources provided by St. Peter Claver’s College through the Belize Culture Fund.

The ceremony also brought together members and representatives of the East Indian Southern Chapter and coordinators of the Yellow Ginger Festival.

World.title: International News: Meet Carina, the $4.74 million cow holding a Guinness World Record
World.content:
International News: Meet Carina, the $4.74 million cow holding a Guinness World Record

By Zoila Palma: A cow in Brazil has made agricultural history after selling for a staggering US$4.74 million at auction, earning her a Guinness World Record as the most expensive cow ever sold at auction.

Carina FIV do Kado, known simply as Carina, is a Nelore cow whose extraordinary value comes not from her meat, but from her exceptional genetics.

Carina had already established herself as one of Brazil’s most prized cattle before her record-breaking sale, Yahoo reports.

She won three consecutive national championship titles in some of the country’s most prestigious cattle competitions before retiring from competition at the age of three. Weighing more than 2,400 pounds, Carina is an impressive example of the Nelore breed, which dominates Brazil’s cattle industry.

Her genetics are what made Carina worth millions of dollars. Her owners can harvest her eggs and sell them to cattle breeders, with each egg reportedly valued at at least US$110,000.

The eggs can be implanted into surrogate cows in an effort to produce offspring with the same highly valued characteristics, potentially allowing breeders to generate award-winning cattle for years to come.

Carina’s record followed another Nelore cow, Mara, who sold for US$4.38 million in 2023. Both cows were bred by Casa Branca Agropastoril, a major name in Brazil’s elite Nelore cattle industry. Due to their extraordinary value, cattle such as Carina receive extensive veterinary care and are reportedly guarded around the clock.

Nelore cattle are prized for their ability to withstand Brazil’s climate, resist disease, reproduce efficiently, grow quickly and perform well without intensive feeding.

World.title: Deal is dead but the march is on: unions confirm Tuesday demonstration
World.content:
Deal is dead but the march is on: unions confirm Tuesday demonstration

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Cabinet’s rejection of the Speednet acquisition has not taken the unions off the streets. The National Trade Union Congress of Belize has confirmed that its planned demonstration for Tuesday remains on schedule, set for two locations at once: the Sir Edney Cain Building in Belmopan and the BTL headquarters in Belize City, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m.

The NTUCB says any change in venue will be communicated over the weekend.

The confirmation is itself the news. The demonstration was originally announced as pressure on the decision, timed to the Cabinet meeting where ministers were expected to take their final position on the proposed BTL acquisition of SMART/Speednet. That position arrived early: on Wednesday, Cabinet announced it does not support the acquisition, effectively killing the deal five days before the planned march.

The unions, evidently, are marching anyway.

The NTUCB’s announcement does not detail the demonstration’s aims now that the deal is off the table, and the possibilities read several ways: a show of appreciation and strength after a campaign that got results, a signal of vigilance to ensure the rejection holds, or a platform for concerns that go beyond the single transaction. The choice of BTL headquarters as a second venue, alongside Cabinet’s doorstep, suggests the unions’ message is addressed to the company as much as the government.

What is certain is the sequence that got here. The NTUCB rejected the consolidation, called the nation to wear black on Friday, and set Tuesday’s demonstration for the decision day. Cabinet moved first, and now the streets get their say regardless.

Tuesday, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., Belmopan and Belize City. Whatever the message turns out to be, Breaking Belize News will be covering both locations.

World.title: One visit too many: man detained over protection order breach
World.content:
One visit too many: man detained over protection order breach

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Toledo District woman has reported her former husband to police for breaching a protection order, after he allegedly arrived at her home appearing intoxicated while the court order was in full effect, and a man has been detained.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 44-year-old woman of Bladen Village visited the Bella Vista Police Station on Friday, August 14, 2026, to make the report.

She told police that on Thursday, August 13, at around 7:00 p.m., she was at home when her former husband arrived at her house, appearing to be under the influence of alcohol. Upon his arrival, according to her report, he went to speak to their daughter.

The problem is a matter of court record: a protection order is in effect for one year, having come into force on January 1, 2026. His arrival at the home, the report states, constitutes a breach of that order.

Police recorded a statement from the complainant and retrieved a copy of the protection order from her. A 42-year-old farmer of Bladen Village was detained, cautioned, and informed of the report of breach of protection order.

The case carries a lesson worth spreading to every household living under the shelter of such an order. A protection order draws a legal line, and crossing it is an offence in itself, regardless of intentions, regardless of who the visit was meant for, and regardless of the visitor’s condition. The order does not pause for special occasions or soften for familiar faces.

Just as important is what the complainant did: she kept her copy of the order, and she reported the breach promptly. Protection orders only protect when breaches are reported and enforced, and hers is the example to follow.

World.title: Farmer, 73, dies in highway collision near Independence
World.content:
Farmer, 73, dies in highway collision near Independence

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 73-year-old farmer has died following a collision between his motorcycle and a pickup truck on the Thomas Vincent Ramos Highway, and police have opened an investigation classified as manslaughter by negligence, the standard procedure for fatal road traffic matters, with the question of fault still to be determined.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Friday, August 14, 2026, at about 7:45 a.m., Independence police responded to a report of a road traffic accident between miles 41 and 42 of the highway, near the Independence garbage dump site.

On arrival, officers found a man lying on his right side on the pavement in an unresponsive state, with an open wound to his head, and a woman sitting at the roadside next to him, crying and complaining of pain. A doctor from Bella Vista arrived shortly after and attended to the man. A black Lifan 150 motorcycle lay extensively damaged about five feet from him, its right indicator still on, while a grey Ford F-150 pickup with a damaged mirror and a minor dent to the right front fender was parked on the left shoulder about fifty feet away.

Police investigation revealed that both the motorcycle and the pickup were travelling in the same direction, from Bella Vista Village toward the Punta Gorda and Independence junction. Near the garbage dump site, according to the police account, the motorcycle’s right indicator came on, and the pickup, driven by a 52-year-old lecturer of Punta Gorda Town, began to overtake. As it did, the motorcycle, ridden by the 73-year-old farmer with a 39-year-old woman as passenger, made a left turn into the right front portion of the pickup, causing the collision that threw both riders to the pavement.

The rider was transported to the Independence Polyclinic, where he succumbed to his injuries. His passenger sustained pain to the body.

The scene was processed and photographed, with a sketch plan drawn and measurements taken, and both vehicles were impounded. The pickup driver was issued a notice of intended prosecution and, upon request, voluntarily provided a urine sample, which was sealed and handed over under chain of custody. The pickup was subsequently inspected by a transport officer and released to the driver.

The matter remains under investigation, and no fault has been determined.

Breaking Belize News extends condolences to the family of the farmer, a man of 73 still working the land and the road, whose morning journey ended a few miles short of the junction.

World.title: San Joaquin Fiesta celebrates 60 years of Faith, Tradition and Community
World.content:
San Joaquin Fiesta celebrates 60 years of Faith, Tradition and Community

By Zoila Palma: The San Joaquin community celebrated a major cultural milestone on August 14 with the 60th anniversary of the San Joaquin Fiesta, marking six decades since the village held its first fiesta in 1967.

The celebration brought together residents, community leaders and cultural stakeholders to honour a tradition rooted in faith, heritage and community spirit.

The National Institute of Culture and History (NICH) was among those supporting the anniversary celebrations and received a special recognition award for its continued partnership with the San Joaquin community in preserving and promoting the longstanding tradition.

The award was accepted on behalf of NICH by Rolando Cocom, Director of the Institute for Social and Cultural Research, and Giovani Pinelo, Public History Officer.

Director Kim Vasquez of the Institute of Creative Arts and members of her team were also present for the celebration.

NICH recognized the leadership of Francisco Magaña of the San Joaquin Fiesta Organizing Committee for his dedication to organizing the annual event and helping preserve the community’s cultural traditions.

NICH also expressed appreciation to its President Albert Vaughan and Minister of Culture Francis Fonseca for their continued support of Belize’s living heritage.

World.title: Franno’s last lap
World.content:
Paul Francis (left) prepares to take the urn with the cremains of his brother, legendary Jamaican track and field coach Stephen Francis, down the red-carpeted track as Sport Minister Olivia “Babsy” Grange (right) and Olympian Asafa Powell (second right) stand with athletes forming a guard of honour at the end of the thanksgiving service for Stephen Francis’s life at National Indoor Sports Centre in St Andrew on Saturday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)Photo: Garfield Robinson

HE spent a lifetime on the sidelines, stopwatch and clipboard in hand, watching athletes take their places on the track, but at the thanksgiving service for his life on Saturday, Vincent Stephen “Franno” Francis was in the spotlight. He made his final lap down a red-carpeted track, his cremains carried in a platinum urn as athletes he had trained and mentored formed a guard of honour — a fitting tribute for the legendary Jamaican track and field coach who produced world beaters.

The emotion was unmistakable as athletes fought back tears while ushering Francis out of the National Indoor Sports Centre, a stone’s throw from the National Stadium where many of them had delivered some of their greatest performances. This time, however, there was no race to prepare for, no stopwatch to start, and no final instructions to give, only the painful realisation that they were saying goodbye to the coach who had spent a lifetime helping them find their way to the finish line, and now they were returning the favour.

For approximately five minutes, sprint legends Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, Shericka Jackson, Kishane Thompson, Elaine Thompson Herah, and many more who spent years being taught the art and science of sprinting stood still as family members, friends, Government officials, and colleagues looked on, reminiscing on the life of a world-class coach.

A nod to his alma mater, Wolmer’s Boys’ School, the sports centre and many attendees were decked in maroon and gold for the four-hour-long service that was enveloped in an atmosphere that swung from grief to celebration.

Pot covers echoed during tributes about Francis’s excellent track record, tears flowed when travelling down memory lane, laughter filled the room at comical moments, and musical tributes and selections provided much-needed comfort.

In his tribute, delivered by Finance Minister Fayval Williams, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness praised Francis for demonstrating what was possible when natural talent was matched with world-class coaching, structure, and preparation. He noted that, through the formation of the Maximising Velocity and Power (MVP) Track Club, Francis helped create a pathway for Jamaican athletes to develop at home, at a time when many were leaving the island in search of training opportunities abroad.

“Athletes under his guidance became Olympic and World champions, record holders and household names. Yet his influence cannot be measured by counting medals alone. He developed people, he established standards, and he challenged athletes to become more disciplined, more prepared, and more demanding of themselves,” wrote Holness.

“He also helped prove that a Jamaican coaching programme could consistently produce performances of the highest international standard. In that sense, his impact reached well beyond MVP. He contributed to the evolution of the Jamaican coaching profession and to a stronger national system of athlete development,” he said.

It was for these reasons that Sports Minister Olivia Grange urged the congregation not to mourn, but to celebrate the man who possessed an extraordinary vision backed by purpose and confidence that what he was doing would bring the results that he envisioned.

“Francis understood that talent was only the beginning. Talent had to be developed, potential had to be channelled, and dreams had to be matched by commitment. That philosophy, my brothers and sisters, helped to shape athletes and contributed significantly to Jamaica’s remarkable place in world athletics. Francis possessed technical mastery. He studied speed like a scientist. Above all, he had a strong belief in Jamaica and the potential of our people,” said Grange.

She added that to honour his legacy, the Government is in discussions to provide student-athletes at the University of Technology, Jamaica, the home of the MVP track club, a scholarship in his name.

The move was welcomed by president of the university Dr Kevin Brown, who thanked Francis for choosing the campus as his training ground and placing the institution on the map, one athlete at a time. He remembered Francis for his bluntness, discipline, and belief in the potential of Jamaica, joking that he never wasted words and advocated fiercely for his athletes.

An emotional Brigitte Foster-Hylton and Asafa Powell, two sprint legends who reaped the rewards of Francis’s brilliance, stood as living evidence of his legacy, though struggling to steady their voices as they fought back tears. Between the emotion, they recalled cherished memories, from dodging train conductors in Italy to travelling in Francis’s old car, thanking the coach who had taken a chance on them, believed in their potential, and pushed them towards global success.

“Everything I became started with one man who saw something in a young man before anyone else did,” said Powell, Foster-Hylton finishing his speech as he broke down in tears.

She thanked Francis for every lesson, sacrifice, laugh, and opportunity, noting that he did not just change her life, he changed countless lives.

“Rest well, Franno. Your whistle might be silent, but your legacy lives on,” she said through tears.

Eulogised by his brother, Paul, who also spoke through shaky breaths, the decorated coach was remembered as a friend, a loyalist, a protector of his athletes, a family man, and a coach.

Adrian Laidlaw wiped away tears as he declared that delivering a tribute to his best friend was the hardest job he was ever tasked with. He said when Francis closed his eyes on July 4, 2026, a piece of Jamaica left with him, and his legacy will always be remembered.

Recounting cherished memories of a man he described as both mentor and friend, MVP President Bruce James said Francis made countless sacrifices in his mission to put Jamaica firmly on the international athletics stage, remaining committed to the vision even in the face of doubt.

James recalled that Francis’s dedication to his athletes never wavered, even from his hospital bed, where he continued asking for updates on their progress — a final testament to a coach whose commitment to his craft and athletes endured to the very end.

“History has proven you right, Franno. The World records, the Olympic records, the World champions, the Olympic champions, the world athletes of the year, the numerous athletes who won medals on the global stage achieved more than they ever thought possible and became better versions of themselves because they were a part of MVP,” said James in a written tribute.

World.title: KFC eats into jerk sales
World.content:
Morant Bay jerk pork vendor Johnny sharing his experience since KFC set up shop in the St Thomas capital town late last year. He told the Observer that before KFC opened its doors he would prepare some 30 pounds of pork each day and most times it would “sell out”. Now he prepares about 20 pounds of pork daily and even that amount is not always completely sold. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

TRADITIONAL jerk vendors in Morant Bay, St Thomas, are reporting a decline in their business since fast food giant KFC officially opened its historic first restaurant in the parish in January this year.

But the vendors say while sales are down they are not being squeezed out of the business which, for years, has attracted residents of the parish as well as scores of people passing through the town.

One jerk pork vendor, who gave his name only as Johnny, last Thursday told the Jamaica Observer that while his business remains open, “it’s not as warm as it once was”.

Johnny, who also works as a butcher, said the business has slowed down and the increase in sales he normally sees during holiday periods did not materialise this year.

He told the Sunday Observer that before KFC opened its doors he would prepare some 30 pounds of pork each day and most times it would “sell out”.

According to Johnny, he now prepares about 20 pounds of pork daily and even that amount is not always completely sold.

He pointed out that even his children sometimes ask for chicken from KFC.

“So I have to go in there and spend to buy what they want,” said Johnny, who added that he continues to receive support from loyal customers who prefer his jerked pork.

Another jerk vendor, who requested anonymity, said the arrival of KFC would naturally result in some loss of business for local food operators, but he does not believe it poses a major threat.

“I don’t know, it would be a downgrade in a sense because most people gravitate towards the KFC and dem business deh,” the vendor said as he told the Sunday Observer that there had been “a slight drop-off” in his business since KFC opened.

“It’s gradually going down, but sometimes it’s up again,” the vendor said, even as he underscored that he welcomes the presence of the immensely popular KFC.

He pointed to the demand for employment opportunities and development in the parish, and described KFC’s arrival as a positive development for the integrated industrial and commercial complex dubbed the Morant Bay Urban Centre.

“People need jobs as well, so I would say it’s a good thing,” the vendor said.

KFC invested $350 million to establish its Morant Bay restaurant which provides jobs for more than 50 people.

The store was warmly received by several residents of St Thomas with one person describing the opening as “a wonderful and historic moment for the parish”.

At the official opening in January, Mark Myers, managing director of Restaurants of Jamaica — the operators of the KFC franchise locally — said the decision to locate in Morant Bay was deliberate and rooted in confidence in the area’s potential.

“This opening is about more than adding another restaurant to the network. It reflects a deliberate decision to invest in communities beyond Kingston and to grow in places where opportunity and potential continue to emerge.

“When plans for the Morant Bay Urban Centre were first taking shape we saw an opportunity to be part of something transformational. We want to participate in the continued development of this parish, to invest early and to grow alongside the community — [and] that conviction is what brought us here,” Myers said then.

World.title: Fears flow in St Thomas
World.content:
Resident Charline Gabas stands in front her home and points to the dirt pushed along the edge of the path where the Plantain Garden River flows in Bath, St Thomas, last Thursday.Photos: Karl Mclarty

JUST over nine months after Hurricane Melissa sent residents of Bath, St Thomas, scrambling from their houses as the Plantain Garden River tore into its banks, washed away a parked car, and threatened to swallow lands inches from their homes, residents say a recent riverbank intervention has done little to ease their fears.

Dirt pushed along the edge in July has provided some protection, residents acknowledge, but they insist it is no substitute for a groyne in and the proper channelling of the river.

Therefore, they are warning that another bout of heavy rain could once again send floodwaters towards their homes, further eroding the riverbank and putting the wider community, including Bath Primary School, at risk.

They are also adamant that another major weather event, similar to Hurricane Melissa which ravaged sections of the island on October 28, 2025, could finally cause their homes to collapse into the river’s path.

When the Jamaica Observer returned to the area last Thursday the scene was markedly different from the one residents had confronted during Melissa’s onslaught last year.

Dirt had been pushed along the edge of the area where the riverbank had broken away, while additional dirt had been placed in the space through which the river flows, apparently to obstruct the water’s path and keep it from pushing towards the vulnerable section.

But for residents who have spent years watching the river steadily eat away at the landscape, the intervention has brought only limited reassurance.

Charline Gabas, who lives in the community at the very edge, acknowledged that the dirt has made the immediate area feel somewhat safer, but said it has not addressed what she considers the fundamental problem — the absence of a proper channel to carry the river away from the homes.

“Don’t get me wrong, enuh, if this was not here I would not be able to stand up here, cause when mi stand up here suh it is a little bit safer. But listen, what we are saying — because we have been here for years — they need to take out that piece and channel it to that dry piece of land over the other side, dig it and carry down there suh so [that] when the river comes down it goes that side and follows that channel instead of come over here. Because with how it stay now, the water is going to come over her same way,” Gabas told the Jamaica Observer.

Last October, as Hurricane Melissa battered Jamaica, sections of the Plantain Garden River bank collapsed, prompting residents living nearby to quickly evacuate their homes. Video footage circulated on social media showed residents fleeing as a section of the riverbank gave way, sweeping away a parked car in the process.

For residents, the episode was not entirely unexpected.

During an October visit, Bath resident Theodore Bailey said the community had been calling for the river to be properly protected for more than two decades. He pointed to cracks in the soil near the threatened homes and warned that the saturated ground could still give way even after the hurricane had passed.

Furthermore, the river’s movement has also changed the landscape over time, according to Gabas who rejected the suggestion that residents had simply built their homes too close to the river’s path.

She said the river was once much farther from the houses and that the encroachment had occurred gradually, as the water continued to wash away the land.

“We could not see river and build we house beside it, we are not that stupid… That is what I am trying to tell people, that the river was all the way over there suh but over time it keep on coming over and washing away the land,” she said, noting that she has lived in the community for 19 years and has watched the river steadily encroach on the land.

Initially, residents had suggested that large boulders be used to strengthen the vulnerable section, similar to measures they had seen elsewhere.

But Gabas said the current deterioration of the riverbank means that approach is no longer enough.

“At the time we ask them fi turn the river and we did a seh get the big stone dem, at that time it never suh bad suh we did a suggest they could use the boulders like wah dem use over Yallahs or Port Royal road [Palisadoes]. But then it get so bad now so that is no longer an option. The river have to groyne back, turn the river and groyne it back,” Gabas said.

Tracy-Ann Emanuel, another Bath resident, said the current intervention does not appear capable of withstanding the force of the river during sustained rainfall. She argued that the river needs to be properly trained — a process that, in practical terms, involves controlling and directing the water’s course so that it does not continue spilling into vulnerable areas.

“Well this nuh mek any sense. They need to rebuild a groyne, this place really need fi groyne back, because if one next big shower of rain come we are going to be in problem, so when PG [Plantain Garden] river a come it a guh push back the dirt fi come over here suh,” she reasoned.

Concerns were also raised about how long it took officials to address the issue. According to Gabas, the work was carried out roughly three to four weeks before the Sunday Observer revisited the area last Thursday.

She said residents had become increasingly concerned as the hurricane season progressed and they saw no work being done yet were given no explanation about who was responsible for the eventual intervention.

She said the lack of consultation has added to the frustration.

According to Gabas, workers arrived, carried out the work, and left without explaining to residents what was being done or what the intervention was intended to achieve. At the time of the Sunday Observer’s visit she said residents did not know which agency had undertaken the work.

Gabas said residents are particularly anxious because relocating is not a realistic option for many of them.

“We cannot move, we nuh have any options. When hurricane came October and we had to move out we things because of what happened and by November I had to move in again [that was one thing], but [now] mi nuh have a next option. Mi nuh have the money to buy land and start over and make a next house again,” she said.

So residents are watching the weather closely and worrying about what another prolonged period of rainfall could bring.

Gabas said the dirt has at least created enough of a barrier to make it possible for her to stand at the edge of the vulnerable area without feeling as exposed as before. But she does not regard that as evidence that the underlying danger has been addressed.

She also pointed to what she sees as a gap between the authorities carrying out physical work and the residents living with the consequences.

Gabas said the Sunday Observer team was the first group, since Hurricane Melissa, to return and speak directly with residents about the condition of the river and their concerns.

“From Hurricane Melissa come last year October unnu a the first set of people who come and have a conversation with we and ask we about the river, nobody else. Anybody else we see, dem just come work and point; dem nuh know we and we nuh know dem. The tractor man seh a work him get fi push dirt and him just a work! The rest a people dem just come in and look, and point finger, and gwaan,” she expressed.

The National Works Agency (NWA) has since been identified as the agency responsible for the intervention work.

Stephen Shaw, the NWA’s manager of communication and customer services, confirmed to the Sunday Observer last Friday that the agency carried out the intervention but said he could not provide details at the time.

For the residents of Bath, however, the immediate concern is less about who moved the dirt and more about whether it will hold when the river next rises.

World.title: NOT TRUE!
World.content:
ANDERSON... perhaps the most serious wound is the suggestion that panels of the court have been constituted or altered in order to secure a particular outcome in a case

Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) President Justice Winston Anderson on Friday broke his silence on allegations surrounding his leadership of the regional body, describing as “entirely unfounded and untrue” suggestions that he interfered with the composition of panels and sought to influence judgments.

At the same time he characterised the disclosure of a series of e-mail between himself and colleague judges to the

Sunday Express newspaper in Trinidad and Tobago “as the most troubling aspect of this entire episode”, and condemned, “in the strongest possible terms, the unauthorised disclosure and publication of confidential material relating to the internal deliberations and confidential correspondence of the court”.

According to Justice Anderson, “such disclosures and their publication are wholly unacceptable and strike at one of the fundamental principles upon which every independent judiciary depends”.

“It erodes trust in the sanctity of judicial deliberations and judicial collegiality. It erodes public trust and confidence in the Third Branch, and it does untold harm to the people we are sworn to serve and betrays the trust and confidence placed in us,” the CCJ president stated.

The Sunday Express had reported that in the e-mail exchanges, a majority of the judges accused Justice Anderson of governing the regional court in an “authoritarian” and “dictatorial” manner.

The complaints, as reported by the newspaper, range from accusations of Justice Anderson unilaterally imposing a judicial dress code to allegations of “panel fixing” and attempts to influence the outcome of cases.

Addressing the allegations further, Justice Anderson said, “Perhaps the most serious wound is the suggestion that panels of the court have been constituted or altered in order to secure a particular outcome in a case.

“Such an allegation strikes at the very heart of judicial independence and public confidence in the administration of justice. It therefore warrants a clear and direct response. The allegation is wholly untrue. No judge of this court can or should be restrained from expressing his or her judicial views, or from deciding any matter according to his or her independent assessment of the law and the evidence,” Justice Anderson stated.

He said that it was “with particular concern” that he “noted suggestions in the public domain” that he has sought to influence the outcome of cases before the court.

“Those allegations are entirely unfounded and untrue,” Justice Anderson declared while explaining that a little known fact is that, “in the original jurisdiction of the court, no dissenting judgments are published”. However, the CCJ president maintained that, “the principle of unanimity is a standard practice in international courts exercising jurisdiction of this type”.

“The suggestion that judicial views were suppressed, or that any judge was directed to reach a particular conclusion, is therefore wholly without foundation. Throughout my judicial career, both as a judge and now as president, I have regarded judicial independence as inviolable. It is a principle that I have consistently defended and will continue to defend,” Justice Anderson said.

Detailing the constitution of panels within the court, the CCJ president pointed out that “the inferential leap required to elevate the issue of Bench attire to an allegation of panel-fixing is irresponsible, intellectually dishonest, injudicious and, quite simply, malevolent!”

“Accordingly, I reject entirely the suggestion that panels of this court have been constituted or altered to secure predetermined outcomes. Such allegations are unsupported by the facts, inconsistent with the court’s long-established practices, and contrary to the principles upon which this court has operated since its establishment,” Justice Anderson stated.

He however said, in putting that matter to rest going forward, “every judge of the court will be required to sit on every panel, unless the judge opts out for a legitimate reason and is excused”.

Responding to reports that he had taken a high-handed approach in deciding on the judicial dress code, the CCJ president provided the background to that development. He conceded that while he “may have approached the matter of the handling of the issue of the dress code too strongly”, he did so because he “regarded it as an institutional issue concerning the appearance, consistency and tone of the court, rather than a question directed at any individual judge”.

Said Justice Anderson: “The CCJ is the apex court for a diverse Caribbean region and population. Dress codes set by the CCJ will have implications for all courts of member states as well as for the region. The idea of individual judges adopting their own interpretation of national or traditional dress would seem to be at odds with the very concept of a Caribbean court.”

He added that “if it is the view of the region that national dress is appropriate for judges to wear on the Bench, the inevitable question of what is ‘national dress’ in a Caribbean context of diversity must be determined”.

“This must be determined by the people of the region and toward this end I propose to engage all national courts in this consultation,” Justice Anderson said further.

Addressing commentary about his meetings and discussions with the president and leader of the Opposition of Guyana regarding the prolonged acting appointments of the chancellor and chief justice of that country, Justice Anderson made it clear that he had “no personal interest or preference in who is appointed” to both positions.

“My concern has always and only been confined to the constitutional principle that the judiciary should be headed by substantively appointed office holders enjoying the full constitutional protections intended by the framers of the constitution,” Justice Anderson insisted. He said while in retrospect he believed “another course would have been much better” his actions were fed only by his concern about “the preservation of judicial independence and the constitutional integrity of the Guyanese judiciary”.

“Those considerations alone informed my actions and comments. They were not motivated by any political or other preference, personal interest, or any desire to intervene in the domestic affairs of Guyana beyond what I regarded as my responsibility as president of the final appellate court for that jurisdiction to ensure constitutional protection of the judiciary,” Justice Anderson said.

On Wednesday, the heads of judiciary of Barbados, The Bahamas, Belize, Guyana, the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, Jamaica, and Trinidad and Tobago — which subscribe to the original and/or appellate jurisdictions of the CCJ — in a media release said, while they “do not consider it appropriate to comment upon the merits of statements or allegations attributed to individual judges, nor upon matters arising within the internal deliberative or administrative processes of the court”, they were gravely concerned “about the breach of confidentiality which resulted in the disclosure of what appear to be internal communications”.

Said the heads of the judiciary: “We remain confident in the Caribbean Court of Justice as a vital regional judicial institution and in the commitment of its judges to the principles which underpin the administration of justice throughout the Caribbean”.

World.title: ‘Dream Supreme’
World.content:
Wards of the state listen during a session at the Child Protection and Family Services Agency Transitional Living Programme Higher Education Day for Youth in State Care and Expo, held inside the Douglas Orane Auditorium, Wolmer’s Boys’, School on Thursday. Photo: JIS

TWENTY-FIVE adolescents leaving State care will receive full scholarships for tertiary education, from Supreme Ventures Foundation under its latest investment in the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) Transitional Living Programme (TLP).

The announcement was made by Chloleen Daley-Muschett, assistant vice-president of public relations and corporate affairs at Supreme Ventures Limited, as she delivered greetings to the TLP Higher Education Day Expo held at Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Thursday.

According to Daley-Muschett, when the foundation first partnered with CPFSA’s TLP in 2021, it awarded 20 youths with full-ride scholarships while it was celebrating its 20th anniversary.

Now that the organisation is celebrating 25 years, Daley-Muschett argued that it was only fitting to award 25 excellent and deserving adolescents with full scholarships to fulfil their academic dreams.

“When we say full [scholarship], we mean full. So tuition, accommodation, expenses, housing, everything, miscellaneous, we provided for them,” she said.

“To date, I can tell you that the foundation has invested more than $100 million. That’s $100 million into the students who have gone through the programme so far. So you can do the math; if it was $100 million for 20, you can do the math to know how much we’ll be investing for the 25 students,” said Daley-Muschett.

That investment, she said, will cover whichever path a recipient chooses, noting that even a traditionally more pricey degree, like medicine, is supported.

“So when I say dream supreme, I mean dream supreme. Don’t limit yourself… If it is something that you’re interested in and you have an aptitude to do, go out there, get the information, make yourself visible, and you never know what can happen for you, because the success of our investment depends on you,” she said.

Daley-Muschett encouraged youth at the TLP Expo to be bold and pointed out that hard work and dedication are the values that will allow them to achieve their goals.

“It depends on your drive, your focus, your own ambition. Those are the qualities that will turn the opportunity that we give to you into achievement for life for you. So to all of you today who are a part of the TLP, this day is for you. The CPFSA has gone all out to have all of these executives here for you. Use the opportunities to ask questions, explore your options, and imagine your future. Don’t limit that imagination. Dream supreme,” she reiterated.

Described as an exit-readiness project, the TLP was implemented through the collaborative efforts of the CPFSA, The University of the West Indies Open Campus, the Caribbean Child Development Centre, and the United States Agency for International Development, which provided the funding for the initial implementation.

The aim of the project is to facilitate a smooth transition to independent living for adolescents who have reached 18 years and are leaving State care.

Under the programme, the TLP youngsters are exposed to different pathways to aid in their readiness for independent living. These include life skills, coaching, entrepreneurship, vocational and technical skills training, house accommodation for two years, as well as tertiary enrolment.
