We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has confirmed that he will seek to have Maciej Berek, a government minister who stepped down this week and who Tusk calls his “right-hand man”, appointed as a judge on Poland’s constitutional court. The move has generated considerable controversy given that Tusk’s ruling coalition has repeatedly pledged to “depoliticise” the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after the previous national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government appointed its former politicians to the court. At a press conference on Thursday, however, Tusk defended the idea, describing Berek as an “apolitical and nonpartisan” figure who would help “fix the Constitutional Tribunal” after it was rendered illegitimate by PiS. Premier @donaldtusk potwierdził, że @MaciejBerek – do tej pory minister ds. nadzoru nad wdrażaniem polityki rządu – będzie kandydatem na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. – To jeden z najwybitniejszych polskich prawników – uzasadnił szef rządu.https://t.co/RsKLhLjHhC — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) August 13, 2026 Berek is a longstanding associate of Tusk. During Tusk’s first period as prime minister, from 2007 to 2014, Berek was head of the Government Legislation Centre (RCL) while also serving as secretary of the cabinet. After Tusk returned to power in 2023, heading a coalition of parties ranging from left to centre right, Berek was appointed as a minister without portfolio and then, in 2025, was made minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of government policy. He has, however, been an extremely low-key figure, rarely speaking in public. Berek is also not a member of parliament, and indeed not even a member of any political party. On Tuesday this week, Tusk unexpectedly announced before a cabinet meeting that Berek, whom he called his “right-hand man”, was leaving the government in order to “move on to other tasks”. The prime minister did not say what those tasks would be, but multiple media outlets reported that Berek would be presented as a candidate to become a judge on the Constitutional Tribunal. Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though was never a member of the PiS party). When Tusk’s coalition came to power, it promised to restore the legitimacy of the TK, including by “depoliticising” it. In 2024, it approved legislation that would have banned anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. However, the measures were referred by the then-president, PiS ally Andrzej Duda, to the TK itself, which subsequently declared them unconstitutional, meaning they did not come into force. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 At a press conference on Thursday, Tusk confirmed the rumours that he would seek to make Berek a TK judge. He called Berek “one of the most distinguished Polish legal practitioners, who has made his apolitical and nonpartisan nature a hallmark”. Berek has a doctorate in law and, between his stints in government, worked as an assistant professor in the department of constitutional law at the University of Warsaw. “For him, compliance with the law and the constitution has always been paramount,” declared Tusk. “I don’t know anyone better equipped, better prepared, to help rectify the situation we face with the flawed Constitutional Tribunal.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: Nie mamy żadnych innych interesów w tej sprawie. Zależy nam na naprawieniu Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, żeby nie był na smyczy prezydenta i PiS-u, tylko wykonywał swoją robotę. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 The prime minister acknowledged that his government had tried to ban politicians from serving on the TK. But he said that Berek himself had recently told him that, “under the current political circumstances, we must do everything we can to remedy the situation” at the tribunal. “Since methods that are unconstitutional are being used from the other side, I must also demonstrate my determination and that we won’t give in to such methods,” added Tusk. Those remarks, in which Tusk also called Święczkowski’s leadership of the TK “embarrassing”, were a reference to the fact that the current PiS-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, and Święczkowski have refused to accept four new TK judges chosen by parliament earlier this year. “We have no interests in this matter other than to repair the Constitutional Tribunal so that it is not a tool and is not under the thumb of the president or PiS, but rather that it performs its work as objectively as possible,” said Tusk. A newly sworn-in @TK_GOV_PL judge says he will not take his seat until four colleagues appointed by parliament are allowed to take theirs. He said their appointments had been blocked "unlawfully", in the latest twist in a long-running disputehttps://t.co/X30rm1Gfzs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 However, there remain major potential stumbling blocks on Berek’s path to the TK, not least doubts over whether Tusk’s coalition partners will support his nomination in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, declared on Tuesday that, if rumours of Berek’s nomination were true, “he won’t get votes from The Left because we promised our voters that politicians wouldn’t end up on the TK”. Given that the government has only a majority of nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition to oppose Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. On Thursday, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. Jeżeli to się wydarzy (a raczej nie), to do niedawna czynny polityk nie dostanie głosów klubu @__Lewica, gdyż obiecaliśmy naszym wyborcom, że politycy nie trafią do TK. Ale IMHO to bardzo krzywdząca dla @MaciejBerek plotka, on by się jako państwowiec w życiu na coś takiego nie… https://t.co/QWFFmdy4V3 — Anna-Maria Żukowska 💁🏻‍♀️ (@AM_Zukowska) August 11, 2026 The next vacancy on the TK’s 15-judge bench is due to open on 18 September, when the nine-year term of Justyn Piskorski, one of the PiS-era judges regarded as illegitimate by the current government, ends. After that, a further vacancy will open in January. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Earlier this week, his chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Radio Zet that Nawrocki would “accept the oath if procedures are followed”. However, he added that he does “not know if [the Sejm] is able to carry out those procedures properly”. World.title: Poland reintroduces VAT cut and daily price caps to lower fuel costs for drivers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has announced that, from Monday, it will reintroduce some of the measures that were used earlier this year to lower prices for consumers at petrol stations amid the energy crisis triggered by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The package, known in Polish as CPN and which will be in place from 17 August until at least 31 August, includes reducing VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and introducing retail consumer price caps on fuels set daily by the energy minister. Announcing the measures on Thursday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said they should result in prices falling by around 1 zloty (€0.23) per litre. Currently, average retail prices are 7.29 zloty for 95-octane petrol and 8.09 zloty for diesel, according to Polish price monitoring service E-Petrol. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Polska będzie w absolutnej czołówce europejskiej, jeśli chodzi o najniższe ceny paliw. pic.twitter.com/ar3IZbzFHQ — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Tusk acknowledged that CPN will entail “serious costs” for the state budget. When similar measures (which also, unlike now, included cuts in excise duty on fuels) were in place between the end of March and end of June, they cost the state an estimated 4.7 billion zloty. On Thursday, the prime minister renewed his criticism of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for last month refusing to sign into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits this year. The government said that the tax, which would have raised an estimated 4 billion zloty, was intended to help cover the costs of fuel subsidies. The profits of many fuel companies have boomed during the crisis, with Polish state energy giant Orlen last week announcing record half-year results. Nawrocki’s chancellery, however, has argued that fuel companies would seek to pass the costs of tax increases onto consumers, thereby increasing prices. CPN was first introduced in March in response to soaring fuel prices in the wake of US and Israeli attacks on Iran and subsequent disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. CPN subsequently helped bring Polish fuel prices to among the lowest in the EU. Since the measures were withdrawn in June, prices at the pump in Poland have risen significantly, placing pressure on the government to again cushion the blow for consumers. E-Petrol reports that prices have recently started to fall, but remain well above the levels seen before the crisis. Economists at PKO, a major bank, wrote on Thursday that higher fuel prices in July, which stemmed from the expiry of CPN and an increase in global oil prices, were the main drivers of inflation accelerating from 2.5% in June to 3.0% last month. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector. It also saw its highest-ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets https://t.co/uhGWJVQvf3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 On Thursday, Tusk claimed that the re-introduced CPN would lead to Poland having among “the lowest prices in Europe”, helping “possibly millions of Polish drivers, on critical days, when they return from holidays”. But he also acknowledged that fuel would “still be expensive”. Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, however, criticised the government for what he claimed was a belated response to high prices. Poland has detained a Russian national who it says was planning to assassinate a person with joint US and Ukrainian citizenship in Warsaw. The news was first announced by Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a press conference on Thursday afternoon. “Thanks to the truly brilliant action of our security services – the Internal Security Agency (ABW) with the assistance of the police – on 7 August we detained a Russian citizen, recruited by Russian intelligence services, whose task was to execute an American and Ukrainian citizen right here in Warsaw,” he said. “This is the first time someone on Russian orders has decided to attack an American citizen on the territory of another NATO country,” added Tusk. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: 7 sierpnia zatrzymaliśmy obywatela Rosji, którego zadaniem było wykonanie egzekucji w Warszawie na obywatelu amerykańskim i ukraińskim równocześnie. Dzięki akcji ABW i Policji udało się temu zapobiec. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Though the prime minister said he was not allowed to name either the suspect or the target, he revealed that the latter was someone who is “inconvenient for Putin’s regime”. Tusk also gave no details of how the assassination was supposed to have been carried out, but said that it was foiled “at the last minute”. In a subsequent statement, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of Poland’s security services, confirmed Tusk’s announcement and noted that the operation to prevent the attack had taken place in cooperation with the US. Police headquarters in Warsaw later revealed that the 29-year-old suspect had been charged with planning a murder and accepting an order to carry out murder in return for material or personal benefit. Both crimes carry jail terms of between two and 15 years. He has also been placed in court-approved pretrial detention. 7 sierpnia br. ABW we współpracy z policją zatrzymała obywatela Rosji, który na zlecenie obcej służby przygotowywał zabójstwo obywatela USA ukraińskiego pochodzenia. Do zabójstwa miało dojść w Warszawie. Operacja była realizowana we współpracy ze służbami USA. — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) August 13, 2026 Poland has been a major target for hostile operations by agents working on behalf of Russia. In February, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the most frequently targeted country in a campaign of sabotage being orchestrated by Russia across Europe. That included an attempt last year to use explosives to derail a train. In June, a Russian artist whose work criticised Putin was assassinated in Poland. Soon after, the Polish security services detained the suspected killer, who they said was using a Georgian passport. Last month, a Russian missile hit Poland during intensive attacks on Ukraine. That followed an incident last year in which around 20 Russian drones violated Polish airspace. Poland has also been one of Ukraine’s closest allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, providing significant military, humanitarian and diplomatic support, as well as welcoming millions of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom remain in Poland. World.title: Polish household assets hit record 4 trillion zloty amid fastest growth in years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poles are building up wealth at the fastest pace in years, with the combined value of household financial assets surpassing 4 trillion zloty (€930 billion) for the first time, according to new data from the Polish Development Fund (PFR), a state entity. The figure reached 4.1 trillion zloty at the end of the first quarter of this year, up 4.3% from the previous quarter, said PFR. That was the largest quarterly increase in just over six years. On an annual basis, assets rose 15.3%, the fastest pace in five years. After deducting liabilities, household net financial assets stood at 3.2 trillion zloty, also a record. Net assets were up 18.4% from a year earlier and 4.9% from the previous quarter. Ponad 4,1 bln zł – tyle wynoszą już aktywa finansowe polskich gospodarstw domowych. To historyczny rekord. W najnowszej analizie PFR pokazujemy, że w ciągu roku wzrosły o 15,3% – to jedna z najwyższych dynamik w historii. Skala i tempo wzrostu aktywów pokazują też, jak duży jest… pic.twitter.com/fSx1yOZtkn — Mikołaj Raczyński (@MikRaczynski) August 7, 2026 The biggest contribution to the quarterly increase came from what PFR classifies as “other equity holdings”, which include shares in limited liability companies, partnerships, cooperatives and mutual insurance societies. They rose by 61.5 billion zloty. Bank deposits recorded the second-largest increase (44.4 billion zloty). Despite the strong rise in equity holdings, bank deposits and cash remained the largest components of household financial assets, accounting for 26.3% and 11.1% respectively. Pension and disability funds accounted for 10.5% of household financial assets. Meanwhile, shares listed on stock exchanges and regulated over-the-counter markets made up 2.9% of household financial assets. Their value is equivalent to 3% of GDP, one of the lowest shares in the European Union, where the average is 8.2%. Although shares make up only a small share of household assets, the Polish stock market has performed strongly in recent years, with its blue-chip index reaching a record high last week and breaking its previous high set 19 years ago. By contrast, Polish households have a relatively high level of cash holdings. Cash was equivalent to 11.5% of Poland’s GDP in the first quarter, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). PFR’s data also show that household liabilities in Poland increased by 5.2% year-on-year to more than 891 billion zloty in the first quarter, well below the rate of asset growth. Long-term loans accounted for 92.2% of liabilities, while short-term loans accounted for 5.1%. Rising household wealth reflects three decades of strong economic growth in Poland, accompanied by a rapid rise in wages and living standards. Earlier this year, state research agency CBOS found that a record 39% of Poles say they are financially comfortable, up from just 3% in the early 1990s. Separate data from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that only 2% of the population live in severe deprivation, the lowest level on record. Poland last year rose to its highest-ever level in a measure of household prosperity in European Union member states, overtaking four other countries. That growth has also fuelled a rapid increase in the number of ultra-wealthy people in Poland, whose number has almost doubled since 2019. However, the PFR data show only total combined household assets and liabilities, not how they are distributed across society. The number of ultra-wealthy individuals in Poland has more than doubled since 2021, a faster rate of growth than anywhere else in the world, according to a new study https://t.co/MNKgmjzn2U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. The personal data of almost 19 million people, including medical information, has been compromised in a major cyberattack on a company that provides services to thousands of medical facilities in Poland. “We are dealing with one of the largest incidents in Poland’s history,” said digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski on Wednesday. He urged people to use government services to check whether their data is affected and to “lock” their national identity number to prevent potential fraud. (￼🧵 1/2) 💬 Dziś doszło do poważnego wycieku danych w firmie MyDr, który może obejmować blisko 19 milionów osób korzystających z opieki medycznej. W związku z sytuacją krytyczną zostały natychmiast podjęte działania mające zabezpieczyć dane i wyjaśnić okoliczności incydentu –… pic.twitter.com/nIp6EvbKiu — Ministerstwo Cyfryzacji (@CYFRA_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026 The attack targeted MyDr, a company that provides services used by many medical facilities in Poland. Its data includes patients’ personal information, as well as medical details such as diagnoses and prescriptions. It was first reported on Monday by Zaufana Trzecia Strona, an IT security news service, which said that it had been contacted on Saturday by the alleged perpetrators, who claimed to have accessed the data of around 18.8 million people. The hackers, who have not been identified, had also sent a screenshot from the compromised database showing the personal data of “one of the most important politicians in Poland”, added Zaufana Trzecia Strona. Shortly afterwards, MyDr confirmed that it had “become the target of an external, deliberate criminal activity involving some of our data”. In an update on Wednesday, it said that, at the time of writing, there was no evidence that the data had been published anywhere. Największy wyciek danych osobowych w historii Polski i co możemy z nim zrobić – nasza analiza incydentu w MyDr i jego potencjalnych skutków.https://t.co/vXUmVfpPAP Opisujemy aktualny stan wiedzy i możliwe scenariusze rozwoju sytuacji. pic.twitter.com/uqhjz1CjZ1 — ZaufanaTrzeciaStrona @zaufanatrzeciastrona@infosec (@Zaufana3Strona) August 13, 2026 Gawkowski addressed the issue at a press briefing on Wednesday. He noted that “there is no indication we are dealing with an external attack…from Russia or any other country”. Poland has recently regularly been targetted by Russian state-linked hackers. It is “very likely” that cybercriminals are behind the attack on MyDr, said Gawkowski, who pledged that there would be an “uncompromising” response from the Polish security services. The minister advised Poles to check in a secure government database whether their data had been leaked. He also advised citizens to use the state web portal, known as mObywatel, to “lock” their identity number, known as a PESEL, which prevents fraudsters from using it. Around 12,000 medical facilities use MyDr’s services, the digital affairs ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The company claims that it processes three million medical consultations and 2.7 million prescriptions a month, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. World.title: Passenger Attacks Four Airport Staff After Being Denied Boarding in Prague
World.content:
A passenger attacked four employees of ground-handling company Menzies Aviation at Prague’s Airport on Thursday evening after being denied boarding on a flight to Rome.

The incident took place at Terminal 2, near Gate C9, shortly after 8 p.m., according to Zdopravy.cz.

The woman arrived late for boarding on a Ryanair flight. After being refused entry to the aircraft, she reportedly became aggressive and attacked members of the ground-handling staff.



One of the employees stepped between the woman and a colleague who was being confronted by her. The passenger then bit him.

Airport police were called to the scene and used restraint equipment to detain the woman. She was subsequently escorted from the boarding area and handed over to the Czech police.

“The woman was late for the boarding gate, and after being denied boarding, she physically attacked an airport employee,” Josef Urban, a spokesperson for the Foreign Police Directorate said.

“Responding officers detained her using restraint equipment, and the case is now being investigated as disorderly conduct,” he added.

The incident was also confirmed by Prague Airport spokesperson Jiří Hánich.

The injured employees required medical treatment following the attack. Four members of the Menzies team were reportedly involved in the incident.

Menzies Aviation has operated at Václav Havel Airport Prague since 1991. The company provides ground-handling services covering passengers, baggage, aircraft and cargo for a significant share of flights at the airport.

World.title: Around 300 Czech Citizens Evacuated Due to Fire in Croatia
World.content:
Some 300 Czech tourists are among the 1,000 evacuees with a Czech police officer sent to coordinate the emergency response.

Croatian prime minister Andrej Plenković is in the town holding a coordination meeting with all emergency services this morning. Croatian president Zoran Milanović is also expected later today.

“All those injured in last night’s fire are being provided with the necessary medical care,” Plenković said in an earlier update on X.

No fatalities have been reported. The spokesman said there were also no reports of serious injuries among Czech citizens.

Some tourists left the area on their own, while others are staying at evacuation centres in Omiš and Split. A Czech consul is on site and is in contact with local authorities and security forces.

Fire spreads across up to 1,000 hectares

Around 160 firefighters, supported by specialised firefighting aircraft, are battling the blaze.

The fire has caused significant material damage, according to eyewitnesses, with dozens of cars and homes reportedly destroyed. Strong winds have helped the flames spread across an area estimated at between 900 and 1,000 hectares.

Witnesses reported hearing gas cylinders exploding inside burning homes, while the streets were filled with the sirens of fire engines, ambulances and police vehicles. Large parts of Omiš have also been left without electricity.

Mass evacuation underway

Hundreds of people have fled the affected area, with some tourists escaping by boat, catamaran and other small vessels.

The organised evacuation is being coordinated through the Ribnjak sports hall in Omiš. From there, evacuees are being transported by bus to the Gripe sports centre in Split.

According to Omiš fire chief Slavko Tucaković, foreigners make up the majority of those evacuated.

World.title: Czech Villages Face Water Shortages as Drought Deepens
World.content:
Residents say they are cutting water use wherever possible, taking shorter showers, reducing garden watering and abandoning plans to fill swimming pool.

Communities across the Czech Republic are struggling with worsening water shortages as wells dry up and small streams disappear after years of increasingly severe drought, according to local media on Thursday.



In the village of Krsy in the Plzen Region, tankers are delivering drinking water daily to a reservoir above the village. Some private wells have already run dry, while others are close to empty.

Residents said they are cutting water use wherever possible, taking shorter showers, reducing garden watering and abandoning plans to fill swimming pools.

Authorities are urging households to connect to public water networks where available.

The shortages are also putting pressure on tourist destinations. In Horni Becva, in the Beskydy Mountains, the population doubles during the summer holidays.

The municipality’s two wells have been operating close to their limits, with firefighters called in to deliver water.

Hotels with wellness facilities are among the largest users, prompting local officials to ask businesses to reduce consumption.

Officials hope conditions will improve when the tourist season ends and autumn rains arrive.

World.title: Burgermeister to Open First Prague Restaurant on Wenceslas Square in 2027
World.content:
Berlin burger chain Burgermeister is preparing to enter the Czech market, with its first Prague restaurant expected to open in early 2027.

The company has chosen Wenceslas Square for its debut. The location will also serve as a base for Burgermeister’s planned expansion across the Czech Republic, with more restaurants already in the pipeline.

Burgermeister has built its reputation in Berlin over the past two decades, growing from a single restaurant in a former public toilet into an international chain with 32 locations across Germany and other European markets.



Burgermeister has not yet revealed the exact address or confirmed a specific opening date.

The Prague restaurant will follow the concept that made Burgermeister popular in Berlin. The chain focuses on freshly prepared burgers and fries, with part of its food production handled in-house. Its operations also include its own bakery.

From a former public toilet to an international burger chain

Burgermeister opened its first restaurant in the Kreuzberg district of Berlin in 2006. The location was far from a conventional restaurant site. It occupied a former public toilet beneath the railway tracks near Schlesisches Tor station.

The unusual setting quickly became part of the brand’s identity. Over the years, Burgermeister expanded beyond its original Berlin location and developed into a larger restaurant chain.

Today, the company has 32 branches and is pursuing its goal of building a pan-European network.

World.title: This Website Tracks How Many Trams Are Still Running Without Air Conditioning
World.content:
A new website is giving Prague residents a live picture of how many trams are operating without air conditioning, highlighting an issue that has become particularly noticeable during the city’s summer heat.

The service, Smrdime.cz, was created by developer Christoph Korb. Its name is a play on the Czech word smrdíme, meaning “we stink,” and refers to the uncomfortable conditions passengers can face inside overheated trams.

The website uses live data to calculate the share of Prague’s trams that are currently running without air conditioning. The figures change throughout the day as new vehicles enter and leave service.

When the service was checked on Thursday, August 13, Prague was experiencing temperatures of around 37 degrees Celsius. At that point, 188 of the 256 trams in operation did not have air conditioning, representing about 71 percent of the fleet being tracked.



Of the 147 air-conditioned trams available, 77 were operating at the same time.

The figures provide a snapshot rather than a fixed daily total. As trams are taken out of service and replaced, the balance between air-conditioned and non-air-conditioned vehicles changes continuously.

The project draws attention to a long-standing issue facing Prague’s public transport system: a substantial part of the city’s tram fleet still lacks air conditioning.

The website is based on data from two publicly available sources. Transport information comes from Golemio, Prague’s open-data platform, while weather information is provided by Open-Meteo. The two data sources are used to calculate the current situation displayed on the site.

Korb built the service with Anthropic’s Claude Code development tool. He has also published the project’s source code on GitHub, allowing other developers to inspect the project and contribute to its development.

World.title: From a Student’s Dream to a Japanese Bakery in Prague: The Story Behind Yaki-Pan
World.content:
For Hoan, opening a bakery in Prague was not a sudden business idea. It was a dream that had been taking shape for more than a decade.

After arriving in Prague as a student, Hoan watched members of the Vietnamese community build businesses across the city, most commonly in restaurants, grocery shops and nail salons.

She worked in grocery stores and restaurants herself, gradually gaining experience in the food industry while studying.

But after finishing school, she still was not sure what kind of business she wanted to open.



One thing was clear: she loved baking.

“Its my dream. It’s been my plan for a long time, more than 10 years,” she says.

Rather than opening another coffee shop, she decided to focus on what she knew best. She had visited bakeries around Prague and noticed what she saw as a gap in the city’s food scene: there were few places specialising in Japanese-style baking.

Around six years ago, she decided that she wanted to fill that gap herself.

The result was Yaki-Pan, a small bakery built around Japanese pastries and flavours. Before opening, Hoan spent roughly a year and a half — and much of that time at home — testing recipes and trying to recreate the textures and flavours she associated with Japanese baking.

Getting there was not straightforward.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Yaki-Pan (@yakipan_brunch)

Learning to work with Czech ingredients

For Hoan, authenticity was essential. She wanted the pastries at Yaki-Pan to resemble Japanese baked goods as closely as possible, but she quickly discovered that one of the most important ingredients presented a major challenge: flour.

Japanese flour differs significantly from the flour commonly available in the Czech Republic. The differences affect the texture, consistency and ultimately the finished pastry.

“The flour here is not the same as when I learnt,” she says.

Instead of simply following recipes she had learned elsewhere, Hoan had to adapt them to local ingredients. She experimented with different combinations of flour and spent months trying to achieve the texture she was looking for.

Three years ago, she travelled to China to study Japanese baking under professionals. There, she was able to work with Japanese ingredients and gain further experience. Returning to Europe meant starting another process of adjustment.

She considered importing Japanese flour to the Czech Republic, but eventually found it difficult to maintain as a long-term solution. Instead, she continued experimenting with locally available ingredients.

“I needed to test for about two years at my home,” she says.

The process has not necessarily ended with the bakery’s opening. Hoan continues to work on her recipes and ingredients, looking for ways to improve the pastries while staying as close as possible to the style she wants to create.

A warm welcome from Prague

If Hoan was worried that Japanese flavours might be unfamiliar to Prague customers, the first day quickly put those concerns to rest.

When Yaki-Pan opened, she had not prepared significantly more food than usual. Within 30 minutes, the bakery had sold out.

The first two months were particularly busy, especially at weekends. Today, the customer base includes tourists, Japanese residents and visitors who have become regulars.

Japanese customers have also played an important role in validating Hoan’s approach, frequently complimenting her on how closely the pastries resemble those they know from Japan.

Among the most popular items is shio-pan, a Japanese-style bread known for its soft texture and salty flavour. At Yaki-Pan, the vegan version has become one of the bakery’s bestsellers and regularly sells out.

Hoan’s own favourite pastry, meanwhile, changes from day to day.

The bakery’s success has also brought an unexpected question. Some customers have asked why a Vietnamese woman decided to open a Japanese bakery.

For Hoan, the answer is simple. “It’s my dream,” she says. “I put all my energy into my recipes.”

Her background, she suggests, is less important than the work she has put into learning the craft and developing the food.

Building Yaki-Pan’s future

For now, Hoan is focused on the bakery she has already built. Yaki-Pan is run by Hoan and her husband, and her previous experience working in restaurants has helped her manage the busy days herself.

The couple are already thinking about the next stage. They hope to add outdoor seating next year and, eventually, open another location.

But there is no immediate rush to expand.

“Now I want to put all my energy into this one,” Hoan says.

There are also plans to introduce another type of matcha, giving customers more choice alongside the bakery’s existing drinks.

For a business that began as an idea Hoan carried with her for more than 10 years, Yaki-Pan remains very much a work in progress. The recipes continue to evolve, customers continue to discover Japanese-style baking, and Hoan is still searching for the ingredients and techniques that bring her original vision closest to reality.

World.title: Prague Taxi Driver Arrested After Taking CZK 3.5 Million Left in His Car
World.content:
A 21-year-old taxi driver in Prague has been arrested after allegedly taking a suitcase containing CZK 3.5 million in cash that passengers accidentally left in his car.

The money was recovered by police after the driver eventually admitted what he had done and told investigators where he had hidden it. He now faces up to five years in prison.

The incident happened in late July, although police only released details of the case several days later.



The passengers were a married couple who had taken a taxi to Václav Havel Airport in the early morning. They were heading on vacation and only realized after reaching the airport that one of their suitcases was still in the vehicle.

The couple immediately contacted the driver and asked him to bring the suitcase back. According to police, he initially agreed, but the luggage never appeared despite further calls and reminders.

The couple eventually reported the matter to police. Given the amount of money involved, forensic specialists from the Prague 1 police precinct joined the investigation.

Investigators quickly located the taxi and detained the driver. A search of the vehicle, however, produced no suitcase.

The 21-year-old initially denied that the passengers had left anything behind, telling police that he had not found any luggage in the car.

His account later changed.

After being placed in a cell, the man confessed and revealed where he had hidden the cash. Police officers and forensic specialists then located the money in a forest near Kladno.

The investigation also uncovered an attempt to destroy evidence. Near the cash, investigators found the burned remains of the suitcase. Police say the driver had taken the items to the forest, piled them together and set them on fire.

The driver remains under investigation and could face a prison sentence of up to five years if convicted.

World.title: Six Prague Rooftops and Terraces to Visit Before Summer Ends
World.content:
Summer is already moving on, and Prague’s rooftop season won’t last much longer.

August is the time to make the most of the city’s terraces, sunset views and outdoor events before they disappear for another year.

Here are six rooftops and terraces worth visiting before autumn arrives.



1. REASON at Masaryčka

Eleven floors above Masaryk Station, REASON offers one of Prague’s newest rooftop dining spots, with views over the city and the Zaha Hadid-designed Masaryčka development.

This summer, its terrace is also home to the seasonal Frerejean Frères Champagne Bar, serving champagne by the glass, cocktails, oysters and light bites. The menu includes THE REASON KIR, made with herbs grown on the rooftop.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and cocktails above Masaryčka.

2. W Prague – ABOVE Rooftop

ABOVE Rooftop at W Prague brings a Mediterranean feel to the top of Wenceslas Square.

The daily Mediterranean Hour runs from 5 to 6 PM, with two spritzes and a Taste of the Mediterranean platter for CZK 990. Oysters are also served from Thursday to Saturday, alongside a programme of summer events and pop-ups.

This summer: Mediterranean Hour, sunset drinks and oysters in the centre.

3. MINUTY Rooftop Terrace

The rooftop at Fairmont Golden Prague offers views across Pařížská, Letná and the city centre from nine floors up.

MINUTY Rooftop Terrace by Golden Eye focuses on champagne, oysters, caviar and cocktails. The terrace is seasonal and is expected to remain open until September, weather permitting.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and caviar with a view.

4. Sky Lounge 360°

For the view alone, Sky Lounge 360° is hard to beat. The rooftop looks across Prague’s historic centre and becomes livelier during the summer months, with DJs, sunset events and Prague Rooftop Festival activities.

It is more about drinks and atmosphere than a long dinner — a good option for an evening that starts at sunset and continues after dark.

This summer: Sunset events, DJs and panoramic views.

5. Casablanca Sky Bar

On the sixth floor of The President Hotel, Casablanca Sky Bar looks out over the Vltava and Prague skyline.

With DJs, cocktails and regular sunset events, it has more of a party atmosphere than a traditional hotel rooftop. It is also one of the venues taking part in the Prague Rooftop Festival.

This summer: DJs, cocktails and sunset parties above the Vltava.

6. Monkey Bar

Monkey Bar at Falkensteiner Hotel Prague is a quieter alternative, with a green, jungle-style terrace close to the main railway station.

Every Thursday until the end of August, the terrace hosts BBQ & Beats, combining barbecue, live music and summer drinks. Frozen margaritas are also on the menu.

For daytime plans, there is Jungle Brunch, including a bottomless mimosa option.

This summer: BBQ & Beats every Thursday through August.

World.title: 5,000 tonnes of stone delivered to Paks: PM Magyar reveals what would have happened without intervention
World.content:
The construction of the underwater weir in the Danube near the Paks nuclear plant, aimed at raising the water levels to ensure supply for the plant, is proceeding on either side of the river on schedule, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Facebook on Saturday.

Fully 5,000 tonnes of stone was delivered to Paks on Saturday alone, Magyar said. Earlier on Saturday, Magyar told a press conference near the cold-water channel of the Paks nuclear power plant that, despite the forecasted drop in water levels, the water level at the plant had risen due to the positioning of two 80-metre barges.

He reported that the controlled scuttling of the barges had begun, and the water level at the pumping station had already risen by 1 centimetre, even as the main branch of the Danube continued to recede.

Magyar emphasised that without intervention, the Danube’s water level would drop so low by Sunday night that one of the two remaining operational turbines would have to be shut down, eventually leading to a complete shutdown.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The cabinet decided on Wednesday to begin the Paks investment project to raise the Danube’s water level, based on submitted plans, expected water level data, and meteorological forecasts. The work consists of two parts: constructing a riverbed sill using 145,000 cubic metres of stone and positioning, securing, rotating, and scuttling two 80-metre barges side by side.

World.title: Sziget attendance plunges as founder warns festival must “move forward to break free”
World.content:
The Sziget festival “must move forward to break free”, its founder, Károly Gerendai, said on Saturday, the final day of the event. “Based on feedback from the audience and the media, the direction we have outlined is good, but many circumstances were not in our favour, so the numbers did not turn out as we would have liked,” he told Hungarian News Agency MTI.

“Our main goal with this year’s festival was to show where we want to go in the future. The reactions show that this test was a success; almost everyone received our efforts favourably. I think we put on a really good Sziget, which can lay the foundations for an upturn next year,” he stressed.

While last year’s six-day festival attracted 416,000 visitors, this year fewer people, around 350,000–360,000, enjoyed the five-plus-two-day event.

“Last autumn, we suddenly had to take over the festival from the departing foreign owners, and then political disputes almost brought Sziget to an end. In the spring, we were optimistic, but we will fall short of the hoped-for numbers,” Gerendai said.

Under the previous owner, London-based Superstruct Entertainment, last year saw a significant loss of 2.8 billion forints (EUR 7.7m), which this year — described as a “break-even” or “investment” year — had been expected to be reduced to 1.5 billion forints with an estimated 400,000 visitors, a target that was not met.

Károly Gerendai. Photo: MTI

The founder added that this is a watershed year, and it was a strategic decision to focus on development rather than cutting costs to avoid losses, as this would lay the foundations for a more successful future. Gerendai said there are three main reasons why the projected loss was higher.

“The organisation and ticket sales started with a four-month delay, whereas previously we had sold a third of our tickets during this early period. The strengthening of the forint made the festival more expensive for foreigners, and the third factor was that among Hungarian ticket buyers, the extreme heatwave, drought, and questions about the power supply created a kind of disaster mentality, which dampened the mood for festival-going,” he explained.

This year, the number of Hungarian visitors increased further, now making up 53 percent of the total, while the number of visitors from abroad continued to decline. Although more people came from neighbouring countries, interest in Sziget declined in its major markets: the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Italy. Israel, Ukraine, and Russia saw a drastic drop due to the wars, and far fewer people came from very distant countries due to rising travel costs.

Gerendai said the decision to involve subcontractors as minority owners in Sziget Ltd had proved successful. He noted that the subcontractors, who have become investors, cover the largest professional areas, including security, cleaning, container, stage, catering, festival infrastructure, lighting, and sound technology companies. “This allows us to have a favourable impact on prices, and also brings in additional expertise, with which we can build a much more professional foundation for construction and development,” he said.

Károly Gerendai. Photo: MTI

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The involvement of Budapest Park gave the festival’s stage for Hungarian artists a prominent place again, he added.

“Bringing back the Hungarian main stage was a really good decision; the audience liked it. There were time slots when the Hungarian bands playing at the same time as the main stage headliners attracted fewer spectators. It is not certain that it was a good decision to have the Twenty One Pilots and Tankcsapda concerts simultaneously, as they are both in the rock category, but there were also counter-examples,” he added.

Gerendai said this year’s main stage concerts were good, with Twenty One Pilots and SOMBR attracting the most visitors. “Unfortunately, the model favoured by the previous owners, based on selling tickets with a strong headline line-up, is working less and less, because many major European festivals can offer strong line-ups. Sziget’s future cannot be based on this alone; at an international level, we need other factors that can make the festival uniquely attractive,” he said.

If you missed it: Shock as young man joins women taken ill en masse at Budapest concert and recounts his ordeal

Among Sziget’s strengths, he said it offered a more diverse cultural experience than most festivals: a multidisciplinary programme, a holiday atmosphere, a unique community experience, good value for money, and Budapest as a world city.

“We will be successful again when we can strengthen our international position, and to do this, we need to rebuild our former network of representatives in 26 countries. It is important that we were able to signal to the Hungarian audience this year that they are just as important to us,” Gerendai said.

He said two major problems had not yet been solved this year, but there had been positive developments.

The capital is expected to start the long-overdue renovation of the K-bridge leading to Hajógyári (Óbudai) Island in the autumn. “The work will take place over two years in two phases, and the reinforcement of the bridge structure is expected to be completed by next summer,” he said.

There could also be a major step forward in making Sziget dust-free. “We have agreed with the mayor that two drilled wells will be created on the island, and one of these can be used to create a continuously sprinkled, watered area in one of Budapest’s largest public parks, which will also have a positive impact on the conditions of the festival,” Gerendai added.

World.title: Tisza Party launches platform for public consultation – reviving name of old show featuring young Péter Magyar
World.content:
Hungary’s governing Tisza Party is preparing to launch a new online platform called Közhang, promising to give people a direct say in national and local issues and allow them to track what happens to their proposals. The name has a curious connection to Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s past: he appeared on an ATV programme of the same name as a young man in 2002.

A new platform for public participation

Tisza Party vice-president Márk Radnai announced that Közhang – described as Hungary’s first community-based social consultation platform – will launch soon.

According to Radnai, the initiative is intended to take the party’s campaign promise of “writing Hungary’s future together” to a new level. The platform will offer continuous social dialogue, with a focus on understandable information, education, transparency and traceability.

The concept is designed to cover both national and local issues. Users will reportedly be able to present their arguments and opinions and follow how a proposal develops – including whether it eventually becomes an actual decision or change.

“Together we write Hungary’s future. But to do this, we now have to take it to the next level,” Radnai said in a Facebook post announcing the initiative.

The website, which is currently not yet operational, displays several slogans, including that it is “Hungary’s first social consultation platform” and encourages users to “not just watch the future, but shape it”.

The site also promises: “Hungary’s future is our common cause” and says the platform will launch soon.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A permanent national consultation?

The concept could represent a significant new channel for public participation under the Tisza government. The platform’s promise of continuous consultation, transparent information and the ability to track how citizens’ suggestions are handled has already prompted comparisons with a permanent version of Hungary’s national consultations.

The website’s domain was reportedly registered by a private individual in January. Radnai has previously been given responsibility for bringing public opinion into government decision-making. In May, Magyar announced the establishment of the Institute for a Functioning and Humane Hungary (MEMI), with Radnai appointed as the government commissioner responsible for the initiative.

At the time, Radnai said the institute would be politically independent and would aim to organise broad public participation without serving party-political interests. Its budget is to be provided by the state.

If you missed it: Hungary unveils huge EUR 3 billion housing plan as new government takes aim at controversial mega-projects

The curious connection to Péter Magyar’s past

The name Közhang is not entirely new to Hungarian audiences. According to Telex, it was previously used by an ATV programme hosted by journalist László Juszt. There is also an unexpected personal connection for the prime minister.

In June 2002, a young Péter Magyar appeared on the programme alongside Ágoston Sámuel Mráz, who later became known as a prominent political analyst. The two discussed former Prime Minister Péter Medgyessy’s past and the handling of Hungary’s communist-era agent affairs.

More than two decades later, the name of the programme is being revived for a platform that the Tisza Party says will give citizens a greater role in shaping political decisions.

Whether Közhang will become a major new mechanism for public participation or effectively function as a permanent national consultation will become clearer once the platform officially launches.

World.title: Good news: Cold front to bring rain and sharp drop in temperatures across Hungary!
World.content:
A cold front will sweep across Hungary on Monday, bringing scattered showers and thunderstorms as well as a significant drop in temperatures – although the eastern part of the country will have to wait until Tuesday for the cooler weather.

After another hot and predominantly dry weekend, a noticeable change in the weather is on the way. According to HungaroMet, the cold front will reach Hungary from the northwest on Monday.

The first significant drop in temperatures will be felt in Transdanubia and the central counties, while the Great Plain will remain hot, with temperatures still reaching around 35°C in several places. By Tuesday, however, cooler air will have reached the eastern parts of the country as well.

The front will also bring scattered showers and thunderstorms, although rainfall will not be widespread. Some areas could therefore see the front pass through with little or no rain.

Temperatures could fall by more than 10 degrees

HungaroMet forecasts temperatures of 12–23°C in the early hours and 27–36°C in the afternoon on Monday.

On Tuesday, the change will become much more pronounced, with morning temperatures expected to range from 11–17°C, while afternoon highs will reach only 23–28°C.

This means that some parts of Hungary could experience a drop of more than 10 degrees compared with the hottest days of the weekend.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Sunday will remain hot and dry

There will be little sign of the approaching change on Sunday for most of the day. The weather is expected to remain predominantly sunny, dry and hot, with only a few temporary clouds developing over eastern and north-eastern areas.

Clouds will increase from the northwest in the late afternoon and evening, however, accompanied by a growing chance of showers and thunderstorms.

Sunday’s daytime temperatures are expected to reach 32–37°C, while overnight lows will generally be between 12 and 19°C. Temperatures could be several degrees lower in sheltered, cooler areas and higher in larger cities and near bodies of water. The southerly wind will also strengthen in places, particularly as the front approaches.

The heat will therefore continue through Sunday, but Monday will mark the beginning of a significant change, with cooler conditions spreading across the country before reaching the east on Tuesday.

World.title: Hungary Weekly Briefing: A new president, the Paks emergency and billions in EU funding
World.content:
Hungary’s post-Orbán transition is moving rapidly from political promises to real institutional change. This week, Parliament elected András Baka as the country’s new president, while critically low Danube levels triggered an emergency operation to protect the Paks nuclear power plant.

At the same time, the new government scored an important legal victory in its attempt to reclaim billions of euros worth of state assets transferred into foundations during the Orbán era — opening another major chapter in Hungary’s political and financial transition.

In the latest edition of Hungary Weekly Briefing, we look beyond these headlines to explain what they mean for Hungary’s future. We examine President Baka’s first messages and the questions surrounding his potentially transitional presidency, the increasingly urgent situation at Paks, and the Constitutional Court decision that could clear the way for the recovery of major public assets.

The briefing also covers the government’s ambitious housing and infrastructure plans, the revival of Budapest’s M3 metro extension, the state of Hungary’s construction sector, Paks II and the latest developments in business and diplomacy.

World.title: Danube drought: Central European countries urged to act together as energy systems come under pressure – analysis
World.content:
The record-low water levels of the Danube are no longer simply an environmental or agricultural concern. A new regional analysis warns that the drought is putting energy security under growing pressure across Central and Eastern Europe – and highlights the need for countries along the river to tackle the crisis together.

The Danube drought has exposed how closely water management, electricity generation, transport and energy security are interconnected. Hungary, Romania and Serbia have been among the countries hardest hit, while Austria, Slovakia and Bulgaria have so far proved more resilient, according to a new analysis by the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs (HIIA).

The study argues that the extreme conditions of summer 2026 have revealed a vulnerability extending far beyond traditional water management. Exceptionally low river levels can reduce hydropower generation, limit the cooling capacity of nuclear power stations, disrupt the transport of fuel and other goods, and increase countries’ dependence on electricity imports.

For the countries sharing the Danube, the crisis also underlines the importance of coordinated regional action. Because electricity grids are interconnected and the river crosses multiple countries, measures taken by one state can affect its neighbours – particularly when drought affects several countries at the same time.

Hungary among the countries hardest hit by the Danube drought

Hungary is particularly exposed because the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, the country’s only nuclear facility, relies on Danube water for cooling. The plant normally provides around half of Hungary’s electricity, making its operation a crucial issue for national energy security.

During the most severe phase of the drought, exceptionally low water levels and unusually warm river water forced Paks to cut its output dramatically. Although a temporary rise in the Danube allowed another turbine to restart earlier this week, the improvement proved short-lived.

The Danube at Paks. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

On 15 August, Paks was operating at only around 25 percent of its capacity, with the government preparing emergency measures to prevent further reductions. Hungary plans to sink two 80-metre barges near the plant to raise the local water level temporarily, while a submerged structure in the riverbed is being prepared as a longer-term solution.

The situation demonstrates the difficulty of replacing nuclear generation at short notice. Hungary has rapidly expanded solar power, while gas-fired generation and electricity imports can help compensate for some of the lost output. However, these sources cannot necessarily replace a large nuclear plant immediately or consistently throughout the day.

The crisis is also raising questions about future nuclear investments. Hungary is reviewing aspects of the planned Paks II project, as the proposed facility would likewise depend on the Danube for cooling.

Romania forced to shut down both nuclear reactors

Romania has faced an even more dramatic situation. The country’s two nuclear reactors at Cernavodă, which normally provide around one fifth of Romania’s electricity, both ended up offline as the Danube continued to fall. One reactor was shut down in late July, while the operator began disconnecting the remaining reactor from the grid on 13 August.

Romanian authorities took extraordinary measures in an attempt to keep the final reactor operating. These included dredging the riverbed, removing a rock obstruction and using rock-filled barges to redirect more water towards the nuclear plant. However, the continuing fall in Danube levels ultimately made a controlled shutdown unavoidable.

Romania declared an energy emergency for August and asked households and companies to reduce electricity consumption during peak evening hours. The government has also increased reliance on other sources, including wind power, hydropower and a lignite-fired power plant.

The shutdown has consequences beyond Romania’s borders. Moldova, which has relied heavily on Romanian electricity imports, now faces the possibility of having to obtain electricity from more expensive alternative sources or introduce power cuts.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Serbia faces both energy and transport problems

Serbia’s challenges are somewhat different but are also closely linked to the Danube. Lower water flows have reduced production at major hydropower facilities, while the river’s role as a major transport corridor has created additional difficulties for energy security.

With water levels exceptionally low, cargo vessels are unable to operate at their normal capacity. This complicates the transport of diesel and other strategically important goods, potentially putting additional pressure on domestic supplies.

According to the HIIA analysis, Serbia has responded by releasing fuel reserves and seeking to strengthen alternative electricity-generation capacity.

The situation illustrates why the Danube drought cannot be treated as an isolated problem affecting individual countries. The same river is simultaneously a source of cooling water, hydropower and drinking water, as well as a crucial transport route.

Austria, Slovakia and Bulgaria have proved more resilient

Austria, Slovakia and Bulgaria have also experienced pressure from the drought, but their energy systems have so far been better able to absorb the shock. Austria has been able to compensate for weaker hydropower production partly through solar and wind generation and increased electricity imports.

Slovakia’s nuclear power plants are less directly dependent on Danube water for cooling because they use cooling towers, reducing their vulnerability to low river levels. Bulgaria’s Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant also has dedicated infrastructure designed to cope with exceptionally low river levels, providing greater resilience than facilities that depend more directly on the river’s flow.

These differences show that the impact of the same climate event can vary considerably depending on national energy infrastructure and the availability of alternative sources.

If you missed it: PM Magyar: Hungary begins sinking two huge barges to raise Danube water levels near Paks

Why countries along the Danube need to act together

The bigger lesson of the 2026 drought is that water security is becoming energy security. The same water resources may be needed at the same time for nuclear cooling, hydropower, irrigation, drinking water, shipping and the preservation of natural ecosystems. As climate change increases the likelihood of prolonged heatwaves and droughts, competition between these needs could become more frequent.

The HIIA analysis therefore points to the need for long-term investment in diversified energy systems, improved water retention, more resilient cooling technologies and stronger cross-border cooperation.

Regional coordination could become particularly important during simultaneous crises. Central and Eastern European electricity markets are closely interconnected, meaning that a shortage in one country can quickly affect neighbouring states. At the same time, when drought hits several countries simultaneously, the countries that normally provide emergency electricity imports may also be struggling with reduced generation.

This means the countries along the Danube have a shared interest in preparing for future droughts together. Coordinated water management, information sharing, emergency planning and electricity-market cooperation could help reduce the risk that a local water crisis develops into a regional energy crisis.

The 2026 drought has provided a grave warning: the future resilience of the Danube region will depend not only on how individual countries manage their own water and energy systems, but on how effectively they can respond together.

For Central Europe, the Danube is no longer just a river running through the region but a critical part of the region’s shared energy and security infrastructure.

World.title: Hungary overhauls tourism: Minister Kapitány announces three major appointments
World.content:
Hungary is overhauling the senior leadership of several key organisations within the Hungarian Tourism Agency (MTÜ) group, with changes announced at Visit Hungary, the Kisfaludy Tourism Support Management Company and the organisation overseeing Hungary’s participation in EXPO 2027.

The changes were announced by István Kapitány, Hungary’s Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy, who said the overhaul was aimed at putting several areas of tourism management on a new footing. The renewed leadership team is being formed under the direction of Olivér Csendes, who was appointed to lead the MTÜ in July.

Three new leaders appointed

According to Kapitány, Andrea Róna has been appointed to head the Kisfaludy Tourism Support Management Company, Andrea Tóth will lead Hungary’s EXPO 2027 organisation, while Botond Boros has taken over the leadership of Visit Hungary.

Kapitány said the government intends to make tourism support and tourism lending more transparent and efficient in order to support the sector’s development. He also praised Csendes’s professional credibility and the trust he has established with representatives of the tourism industry, saying these provided a strong foundation for achieving better results.

New plans for Hungary’s EXPO 2027 participation

One of the most significant announcements concerns Hungary’s participation in EXPO 2027 in Belgrade. Kapitány said the government would not automatically continue with the concept inherited from the previous administration. Instead, it will develop a new plan based on professional and financial considerations.

The government also plans to launch new public procurement procedures, with the stated aim of creating genuine competition between multiple bidders and securing the strongest professional results.

Closer cooperation with the tourism industry

The minister said the government would maintain close professional dialogue with representatives of Hungary’s tourism sector, as well as with the Ministry of Transport and Investment. The changes come as the new MTÜ leadership seeks to accelerate decision-making and introduce changes across several areas of tourism policy.

Csendes was appointed to lead the Hungarian Tourism Agency on 21 July. He previously served as CEO of Visit Hungary and as director of digital and innovation at the Austrian National Tourist Office.

Kapitány said the first week under Csendes’s leadership had already seen numerous initiatives launched, suggesting further changes could follow as Hungary seeks to reshape the management and support of its tourism industry.

World.title: Fires break out across Szeged in Hungary, railway traffic halted near blazes
World.content:
Several fires broke out in and around Szeged on Saturday, with firefighters battling flames across thousands of square metres and railway traffic temporarily suspended because of one of the incidents.

One of the largest fires was reported near Vértói Road and Merkúr Road, where dry grass and fallen leaves caught fire alongside the railway tracks. Firefighters from Makó, Ruzsa, Hódmezővásárhely and Kiskunmajsa were deployed under the direction of the Csongrád-Csanád County disaster management operations service.

The flames threatened a nearby solar park, but firefighters managed to prevent the fire from spreading to the facility. Railway traffic between Sándorfalvi Road and Vértói Road was also suspended temporarily because of the fire. The flames were surrounded using six water jets.

Hay bales and buildings also catch fire

Firefighters were also called to Erdőszéli Road, where around 60 large round hay bales caught fire. A shed and a trailer also caught fire in the incident. Firefighters from Szeged and Kistelek managed to extinguish the flames and were carrying out follow-up operations.

The fire involving the bales is expected to require additional work as crews separate the piles to deal with the remaining hot spots.

Woodland vegetation catches fire

Another fire broke out along Bordányi Road, where approximately 2,000 square metres of woodland undergrowth, dry grass and fallen leaves caught fire.

The flames posed a threat to an unoccupied farmstead, but firefighters were able to contain the situation. Crews from the Szeged professional fire service continued working at the scene, with firefighting water supplied by a local volunteer association’s water tanker.

Authorities warned that operations at the site could continue for an extended period.

Dry vegetation increases fire risk

The incidents show the heightened fire risk created by dry vegetation during the summer. Firefighters were required to respond to several separate locations around Szeged within a short period, including another vegetation fire along Vértói Road covering roughly 1.5 hectares.

The emergency services deployed crews from several surrounding towns to deal with the outbreaks and prevent the flames from spreading to nearby infrastructure and buildings. Residents in the affected areas are advised to follow instructions from emergency services and avoid approaching active firefighting operations.

World.title: Romanian swimmer David Popovici claims third European 200m freestyle title after 100m triumph
World.content:
Romanian swimming star David Popovici has won the 200m freestyle race at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris, his third consecutive European title in the event.

The win on August 14, following the August 12 gold in the 100m freestyle race, makes him the only athlete to have won both races at three consecutive editions of the European championships.

The 21-year-old Romanian swimmer finished the race with a time of 1:44.15, 0.40 seconds ahead of runner-up Tomas Navikonis of Lithuania, and 0.72 seconds ahead of Britain's James Guy.

In the 200m freestyle event, Popovici also won the Olympic gold in Paris in 2024, as well as two world titles, in Budapest in 2022 and in Singapore in 2025.

His personal best in the 200m freestyle came at the 2022 European Championships, when he clocked 1:42.97, the third-fastest time in history.

World.title: Romanian executive to submit fifth payment request under Recovery and Resilience Facility
World.content:
The Romanian government is set to submit the fifth payment request under the EU-backed Recovery and Resilience Facility, or PNRR, according to an announcement from European Investments and Projects minister Dragoș Pîslaru.

Payment no. 5 is worth EUR 2.84 billion, and is the penultimate request that Romania will submit within the PNRR. Once approved, the fifth payment will bring Romania’s absorption rate of PNRR-related grants to 78%, from 66% currently.

“One final request remains, request no. 6, worth EUR 2.58 billion in grants and EUR 1.76 billion in loans. From a total of EUR 13.57 billion allocated at the time the PNRR was signed, we will reach EUR 10.56 billion after request no. 5,” Pîslaru said during a press conference.

Initially, the European Commission planned for a single final payment request, reuniting the now separated requests no. 5 and 6, the minister noted.

The final payment request will be submitted at the end of September, and with it “we could reach 97.2% of the PNRR,” he said, referring to the grants component.

“47% was the percentage of the PNRR when I came to the ministry, after four years since the program was launched. The annual average was about 10.4% of the PNRR. In one year and two months, under the Bolojan government, we added 31% of the PNRR,” the minister also said.

Romania’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan is financed through EUR 21.41 billion under the EU mechanism, including EUR 13.57 billion in grants and EUR 7.84 billion in loans. The fourth payment request, worth EUR 2.62 billion, was approved by the European Commission in May of this year.

World.title: Drone crashes in Romania’s Tulcea County
World.content:
A drone crashed on Friday, August 14, in the area of Luncaviţa, a locality in eastern Romania’s Tulcea County, about five kilometers from the border with Ukraine, the Defense Ministry (MApN) announced.

The drone crashed in a wooded area and caused no casualties, according to preliminary information provided by MApN.

The drone was not detected by MApN’s radar surveillance systems as it was flying at a very low altitude, the ministry said.

The crash resulted in an explosion followed by a fire, which has been extinguished, the Emergency Situations Inspectorate of Tulcea announced.

A MApN team, using an IAR 330 PUMA SOCAT helicopter, will investigate the area.

A day earlier, drone remains were discovered in the sea, close to Romania’s Costinești beach, on the Black Sea shore. Five drones were tracked nearing Romanian territory on the night of Wednesday, August 12, to Thursday, August 13, around 1 AM. One drone briefly entered Romanian airspace in Tulcea County but then exited and headed to Ukraine. Another drone was detected in Romanian airspace around 9 AM. Earlier this week, two Gerbera-type drones were destroyed by divers of the Romanian Army in the exclusive economic zone, approximately 165 kilometers from Constanța, in the Neptun Deep exploitation area.

At the end of the August 14 government meeting, prime minister Ilie Bolojan said the country’s military was doing “everything in their power to combat the drones.”

“We have a reality that we cannot deny, namely that the war resulting from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is having an impact, including along our borders, and we can expect drone debris, drones reaching the river areas along Romania’s border, in the vicinity of ports, to stray into Romania,” the PM said.

“It is regrettable that we are facing such situations, but given what has happened in recent months, we are beginning to see that this is becoming something of a constant; it is not just in Romania, we have seen what has happened in other areas as well. It is becoming clear that equipping our Armed Forces as quickly as possible with counter-drone systems is a necessity,” he added.

World.title: Romanian telco Digi reports 10% higher revenues in Q2 2026
World.content:
Romanian telecommunications company Digi (BVB: DIGI) reported consolidated revenues of EUR 608 million in the second quarter of 2026, representing an 11% YoY increase.

Adjusted EBITDA (ex. operating leases) for Q2 2026 increased by 23% compared to the result from Q2 2025, reaching EUR 169 million. Consequently, in the first semester of 2026, the group recorded consolidated revenues of EUR 1.2 billion, a 10% increase versus 6M 2025, and adjusted EBITDA of EUR 398 million, up 17% YoY.

“Spain continues to be our primary growth engine, maintaining strong commercial momentum and progressing in line with our long-term plans, while Romania continued to perform well,” said Serghei Bulgac, CEO of Digi Communications.

Last month, Digi successfully completed an initial public offering for its Spanish subsidiary. The Spanish IPO was multiple times oversubscribed, showing investor appetite for the company’s shares.

In Q2 2026, Digi reached 33.9 million revenue-generating user agreements (RGUs) across Romania, Spain, Portugal and Italy, a 14% increase compared to Q2 2025.

The mobile segment stands out for generating the most RGUs within the group’s array of services, accounting for 51% of the overall clients across the four markets. In Q2 2026, the mobile segment saw its RGUs climb to 17.3 million, a 19% YoY increase, covering mobile telephony clients across Romania, Spain, Portugal and Italy.

In Romania, the mobile service segment remained the largest, reaching 8.4 million RGUs as of the end of Q2 2026, a positive evolution of 20% compared to Q2 2025. Broadband services registered an increase of 4% in Q2 2026, compared to Q2 2025, up to 5.2 million RGUs, while the segment of Pay-TV services (cable and satellite) increased by 2% YoY, up to 6.1 million RGUs. Together with fixed-line telephony, the total number of RGUs in the Romanian market amounted to 20.5 million customers as of Q2 2026, a 9% increase versus Q2 2025.

Spanish operations continued the strong performance in Q2 2026, with the number of users of fixed services, internet, and mobile telephony increasing by 23% compared to Q2 2025, to 11.9 million RGUs. Mobile users increased by 19% to 7.8 million RGUs, while broadband users increased by 28% to 2.9 million.

In Portugal, the number of RGUs amounted to 960k, up 22% YoY, of which 545k were mobile, and 186k were broadband users.

In Italy, mobile users increased by 4,5% YoY, reaching 535k RGUs as of the end of Q2 2026.

In the United Kingdom, Digi launched its fiber broadband services and continued expanding its network footprint during the second quarter of 2026, while onboarding its first customers.

World.title: Romania’s Presidential Administration to host summit on animal welfare
World.content:
The Presidential Administration will host the second edition of Animal Summit Romania on September 29 - 30, Diana Pungă, a state adviser for relations with civil society at the institution, announced on Friday, August 14.

The event, organized by the non-profit Sache Vet Association and Bucharest’s Animal Protection Administration ASPA, will take place at Cotroceni Palace.

Over two days, it will gather public administration representatives, veterinarians, legal and education specialists, non-governmental organizations and other experts to discuss animal protection and welfare and solutions to challenges in the field.

“Romania continues to face major challenges in the field of animal protection. Beyond the issue of abandonment and the lack of education about responsible pet ownership, civil society frequently raises concerns about the non-transparent operation of some private shelters, suspected abusive euthanasia practices and difficulties in uniformly enforcing existing legislation. In many communities, volunteers, NGOs and active citizens end up compensating for the lack of coherent institutional mechanisms by becoming directly involved in animal rescue, shelter monitoring and the promotion of responsible sterilization and adoption,” an announcement from the organizers reads.

All of these aspects point to an urgent need for clear standards and consistently implemented public policies protecting both the communities and the animals, the organizers said.
